sections.section: Dartvel — The Complete Vision, to be implemented

sections.absent: A box can be turned now, and could not: the chain faded, rounded, bordered and painted a gradient through a box and had no way to rotate one, so a design tilted badge and its angled price flash came through square -- rendered, plausible, and not the design, which is the kind of loss nothing reports. rotate takes degrees rather than radians, deliberately differing from Transform.rotate, because the number in a page document, the number a designer reads in an inspector, the number Figma reports for a layer and the number in exported source are then the same one, converted once where the widget is built; the parameter is named for its unit so somebody reaching for radians sees it before running it, pi over four in degrees being very nearly no rotation. Zero is not a rotation, since a Transform that turns nothing would be a layer in the tree of every page for the one design in ten that tilts something. Text can be underlined and struck through now, and could not: the chain carried every other text style a design uses -- size, weight, family, colour, letter spacing, line height, line limit, overflow -- and had no way to mark a link or a superseded price, so both arrived as ordinary text, which is the same silent loss the missing rotation was. One method taking Flutter's own TextDecoration rather than an underline flag and a strikethrough flag beside each other, matching overflow(TextOverflow) already on the chain: a design that underlines and strikes the same run is a real design, and two flags cannot say it. Text nobody decorated carries no decoration at all rather than TextDecoration.none, because naming none would override an underline an enclosing theme asked for, which is a decision the chain was never given. A box can be blurred now, and could not, which cost two different designs: a soft-focus decorative shape rendered sharp, and -- far more commonly -- a frosted card over a photograph rendered as a flat translucent panel. Two methods rather than one, because they are not the same picture: blur softens the box and what is in it, backdropBlur leaves it sharp and softens whatever shows through, which is the whole of the frosted effect, and a single blur() would have to guess which was meant. The unit is a standard deviation, which is what ImageFilter.blur takes and what CSS's blur() takes, and Figma's own CSS export writes the number from its Layer blur straight into blur(Npx) -- so the value a designer typed is the value in the document, in the chain and in the exported source. A background blur is bounded by the box's own corners, since an unclipped backdrop filter blurs the whole screen behind it: the page goes soft and nothing points at the card that asked for it. Nought is not a blur, for the reason nought is not a rotation -- a filter layer that changes no pixel costs what a real one costs -- and a negative one is refused before ImageFilter.blur asserts on it and takes the page down over a number a document can carry. The chain also reaches text now, and did not. DVText drew text and only text: a modifier carrying padding, a background, a corner radius, a border, a width or a fade reached it and did nothing, on a build that succeeded. This repository did it to itself four times -- the studio's Close button and a tab label, both asking for padding round a tap target and getting the glyphs; the site's own paragraph helper, whose maxWidth was the readable measure every paragraph on dartvel.dev was supposed to be held to and was not; and the framework's own prebuilt sign-in page, whose Sign in button asks for padding, a corner radius and a dark fill and rendered as the two words on their own. The test over that page expected exactly one DVBox and passed because of it, which is a count measuring the bug rather than the page; it now asserts the fill and the radius reach a decoration. There is a fifth, and it is the one with a claim attached: a page document says a text node is centred with align, that becomes DVModifier.align, and DVText looked straight past it -- so every centred heading in every imported design came through left-aligned while the feature list said centred text survives the import. That is the same shape as the bug the semantic fields had on this widget before they were read: the call goes where it naturally goes and the widget it goes to never looks at it. The box half is drawn by the thing that draws boxes rather than by a second copy of the code here, only when one was asked for -- a container round every DVText in every application, for the styling most of them do not use, is a cost nobody chose -- and the tap and the semantics are cleared on the way, because text already applies them and its handling of a role that owns its own label is the careful one. Left in, the box would carry them too: a callback that runs twice and a screen reader saying heading, then heading. A rounded box also rounds what is in it now, and did not: the radius reached the decoration and nothing else, so a box drew rounded corners and its child squared them off again. With a flat colour nobody notices, because the decoration is the only thing painted there. With a photograph everybody does, and it is the commonest rounded thing in any design -- every circular avatar came through as a square photograph inside a rounded outline. Clipped only where a radius was asked for, and in both the animated and the plain branch, because a rule applied to one of two is a box that clips until somebody asks it to animate. A box can also be told to crop what is in it without being rounded, which is its own decision in a design and the commonest version of it is a photograph cropped by a square frame. Without that the child paints outside the box and the page carries an overflow stripe, so an imported design arrives visibly broken rather than quietly wrong. Hard edges on a straight edge and antialiased on a curve: a rectangle needs no smoothing, and paying for it on every cropping frame is a cost with nothing to show for it. A border can be on one side now. The document could say a colour and a width and the width went to Border.all, so a box with a rule under it was a box with a line on all four sides -- not a missing style but a wrong one, and the commonest border in any design is a single hairline under a header or between two rows. Four widths beside the colour, in the shape the corners and the shadow already use: the colour owns the decision and the sides are its companions, because a side applied on its own is a line nobody chose a colour for. A document that names no side still draws all four, since one width has always meant a box and every page written that way has to keep meaning it; a side named as nought is not a side, because a BorderSide of no width renders as nothing and reads in the exported source as a decision. A page document can also name a wrapping row now. Three separate switches read a layout name -- the renderer, the Dart exporter and the editor's own canvas -- and a fourth list, the palette, decided what anybody could drag in. The wrapping row was missing from all four while DVBox.wrapLine had existed the whole time, so a chip row or a tag list, which is the commonest wrapping thing in any design, came through as a single row that runs off the side of a phone. The drift was silent because an unknown name falls through to a column in every one of them. There is one catalogue now and the palette is built from it, the way the palette was already built from the leaf types; the column keeps the label people call it, because its name in a document is list -- it is the default, and a page written before there were others has no layout at all. A wrapping row is aligned like any other row, which took a second change and would have been the same bug one level down: the alignment properties are written for every auto-layout frame, so a wrap that ignored them would be a property the inspector offers, the document carries and nothing applies. DVBox.wrapLine hard-coded start and gave a Wrap no alignment at all. A Wrap offers every alignment a row does, so the mapping is one for one and a wrapping row aligns exactly like the row it becomes when the line has space; stretch is the exception and becomes start, because a Wrap has no equivalent -- its children are as wide as they are, and there is no width to stretch them to. The surface a page is edited on draws it the way the page does now, and did not. "What is edited is what ships" is what the renderer's own documentation promises, and the canvas built its containers itself -- a switch over the layout name and nothing else. No padding, no background, no radius, no border, no shadow, no spacing, no alignment, and a stack piled its hand-placed children into the corner. So a card was a bare column while somebody was styling it and a card once the page ran, and the person doing the styling could not see what they were doing. Both surfaces call one layout function and one styling function now, which is also what removed the third reader of a layout name. The styling travels to the canvas and the behaviour does not: a canvas that navigates away when somebody taps the card they are editing is worse than one that shows the card unstyled. A grid can also be told how many columns it has. The renderer read that, the exporter wrote it, and a document could override it per breakpoint, while the inspector offered no control for it at all -- so a grid built in the builder was permanently two columns wide. It is the drift the layout-property list exists to prevent, in the layout-property list, and the guard over that list could not catch it because it asserted a set of names it already knew about. A layout property now says which layouts it means anything to, and the inspector offers it only there: a row has no columns, and a control that does nothing is worse than one that is absent, because the person who set it has decided something. The export guard holds each one to a layout it belongs to for the same reason. Absent: nothing named here.

A model is discovered by a pattern over its source, and that pattern could not read its own annotation twice over. It stopped at the first close parenthesis, so a string argument containing one -- schemaType: 'Product (beta)' -- ended the annotation early and the model was not found at all: no generated class, no table, no admin row, no graph node, no static paths, on a build that succeeded. Six parsers carried that pattern -- the model generator, the project graph, the admin scaffold, the schema snapshot, the static-paths generator and the kiosk check -- and a model one of them missed while another found it is a table in the database with no row anywhere else. Each is now matched against a copy whose annotation arguments are blanked to spaces, which keeps every offset so the arguments themselves are still read from the original. The same scan skips string literals and comments, because an annotation described in prose is not an annotation: the marketing site describes one in a paragraph above the annotation its page carries, and a parser that searched the file for the first occurrence read the paragraph. Absent: nothing named here yet beyond what the sections for forms, model pages and multi-tenancy record.

Both @DVBackendCron and @DVClientCron are collected into generated entries, and nothing ran either until this was written. The note here used to say DVScheduler ran them; it did not. DVScheduler was instantiated in exactly one place in the repository and that place was its own unit test, so a schedule travelled from an annotation into a generated list and stopped. The generated schedules file now emits the handler behind each backend entry and a starter that registers them and ticks, and the generated startBackend calls it before it serves. The client half is a second file for a reason -- the generated backend imports the backend one, and a client schedule declared on a page would pull Flutter into a server with no dart:ui, which a show clause does not prevent because the whole library is still compiled -- and the generated client runtime starts it. An application with no schedule starts no timer on either side. A schedule now says for itself whether the occurrences missed while the process was down are run when it comes back, and the annotation could not say it before -- the scheduler took catchUp per task from the day it was written, and the only way to reach it was the hand-written register call that generated schedules exist so nobody writes. Nullable rather than defaulted, because a schedule that wrote false has decided about itself and must outrank the blanket setting a starter is called with, while one that said nothing is leaving that decision to the application: a nightly digest sent four times the morning a server comes back is worse than one digest missed, and a rollup that writes a row per period wants the opposite. The expression is also no longer the whole of the annotation, which is the part that could have failed quietly: the collector's pattern required it to be, so an argument after it did not make the schedule wrong, it made the function stop being a schedule at all. A catchUp the generator cannot read as a literal stops the build rather than being treated as unstated, since the generated entry carries the value rather than evaluating it. A client tick is a wakeup as well as a tick, and that is taken into account now. A timer firing every twenty seconds from somebody's pocket wakes the device for a schedule that could have waited, and the system suspends the timer anyway -- so the periods that passed while the application was away arrived whenever it happened to fire next rather than when it came back. The client ticks only while the application is in front of somebody, stops when it goes away, and ticks once on the way back, because whatever came due while it was away is due now rather than up to the interval from now, and that wait is the whole of what somebody who just opened the application is waiting on. An application that declares no client schedule gets a starter that starts nothing and listens to nothing, since a lifecycle subscription in every application is the same cost as the timer this file already refused to start. Reaching the application lifecycle is also why the client schedules are a file of their own: DV lives in dartvel_flutter, and the generated server reads the other one. Absent: the per-target capability report. DV.Schedules.capability, its granularity/whenBackgrounded/whenTerminated record, the doctor finding for an interval finer than a target honours, and DV-CRON-001 to 004 are designed and unbuilt. What ships is the generated registration and ticking described above, whose platform behaviour is now stated per target rather than implied by the annotation.

nothing now, and something was. Seven adapters -- in-memory, database, Redis, SQS, RabbitMQ, Pub/Sub and Kafka -- and the four network ones are verified against a real broker in CI rather than against a fake. Six of the seven were also unimportable until recently: of eight files under src/queues, exactly one was exported from the public entrypoint, so DVSqsQueueAdapter, DVPubSubQueueAdapter, DVKafkaQueueAdapter, DVAmqpQueueAdapter and the transports behind them were public classes no application could reach without writing a package:dartvel_core/src/ path. The tests reached them that way, which is why nothing noticed. They are exported now, and a reachability check in CI fails a section citing a file nothing can call. Absent: DVJobState.completed, which nothing produces. A job that finishes is removed from the queue rather than marked, and the admin counts pending and failed and never asks for completed -- so an application switching on the state will never see that branch taken. Retaining finished jobs to make it reachable would grow without bound, and no retention policy is specified, so the value is named as unreachable rather than given behaviour nobody chose.

Policies are typed, registered and default-deny: DV.Auth.authorization.can returns false for a policy nobody registered, which is the right answer to a question the application never taught it to answer. What this section claimed and did not do until 2026-09-06 is the page half of it. @DVPage has taken a policy since the annotation was written and the specification gives it as one of the two usage examples, and the generator never read it -- the string was parsed in exactly one place in the repository and that place was the backend function generator, while route guards came from a directory convention. So a page carrying the annotation for guarding it was open to everybody and nothing anywhere said so, which is the worst shape an authorization bug takes: an unguarded page that looks unguarded is a decision somebody made, and one carrying the annotation is a developer who has already ticked it off. It is enforced now. The generated router calls one runtime checker rather than an inlined auth call, because a router emitting the exact shape of that surface would pin it into every generated application; a page whose application has configured nothing to answer the policy is refused rather than opened, since treating no answer as yes would reintroduce the same bug as a default instead of an omission; and a directory guard still runs first with the policy after it, because a page can be under a guarded folder and carry a policy of its own and replacing the chain would quietly drop the folder's guard. A policy that is not a Dart reference is refused at build time, since the value is emitted into generated source where anything else either fails to compile or compiles into something nobody wrote. A first attempt at fixing that did not fix it, and this record said it had. The guard builder, the runtime checker and a unit test for each were written and committed, the index was updated to say the router called them, and nothing did: the live generator's own page-argument parser still never read policy, the runtime checker was not exported from dartvel_flutter, and no code outside those two files referenced either symbol. Asserting on the shape of a string returned by an uncalled function is what let it pass. It is wired now -- the generator parses the argument with the same function the test holds to account, the route carries it, the redirect the router emits calls the checker, and the checker is exported. The backend half is built too, and this entry went on saying it was not: a policy on a backend function is parsed, emitted as a gate on the generated route, and answered by the same default-deny surface -- the gate runs after the body is read so CSRF still runs first, and inside the route rather than around the router, because a policy belongs to one function. The last thing this section wrote down and did not do was @DVPolicy(ModelType) itself. It is the specification's headline example of authorization and it appeared in exactly one file in the repository: the one declaring it. So a developer could write a PostPolicy, watch it compile, and have every question about a post answered by default-deny -- the right direction to fail, and still an authorization model that is written down and not the one running. A policy class's conventional methods are registered now, by the client runtime before a page can ask whether to draw an action: a generated table hides an action the policy denies, and a client that registered nothing would hide every one of them. The generated server does not register them, and the first attempt at this had it doing so until the integration job refused to compile the result. A policy is written against the application's models, application code is told to reach those through the generated barrel, and that barrel exports the router and the generated widgets -- so one policy import compiles Flutter into a server with no dart:ui, which is the reason the client schedules already live in a file of their own. The server enforces the policy on a backend function instead, by name, through a surface that imports nothing of the client's. The registration tears the method off rather than wrapping it, so Dart infers the user and resource types from the policy's own signature and the registry key is the type the policy actually takes rather than a string this generator assembled. What the annotation's own argument is for is the disagreement: a method on @DVPolicy(Post) that takes a Comment stops the build, because it would register the check under Comment -- Post keeps failing closed while Comment is opened by a policy nobody wrote for it, and neither half of that says anything out loud. A method that takes no resource is refused for the reason the API has one: can(user, action, resource) always carries a resource and the registry is keyed by its type, so a check without one could never be reached by the question it answers. A method that is not a conventional action is left alone rather than registered under its own name, which would put a key in the registry nothing asks for and turn a typo into a policy. Absent: the generated components asking a policy before they draw an action, which this section of the specification also writes down. Model.Admin draws New and Delete and a form that saves, and consults nothing, so somebody a policy forbids to delete still sees Delete and pressing it deletes the row. Named rather than half-built, because the check needs a user and there are two notions of one here that nobody has reconciled: DVAuth.currentUser is a DVAuthUser, and a policy written the way the specification writes it takes the application's own User model. register casts the user to the type the policy declared, so handing it the session user would throw at the moment of the check rather than deny -- a crash where a refusal belongs, which is worse than the gap. What is missing is a way for the framework to know which model is the application's user, and that is a decision rather than an omission.

The nineteen DVMiddlewares keys ran nothing until this was written. @DVUseMiddleware had one reader in the repository -- a validator in the backend generator that threw when a name was not on a whitelist -- so it checked the spelling and dropped the list. Nothing was stored, nothing reached the generated router, and no request was ever handled differently for declaring any of them. The implementations were not missing either: rateLimit, securityHeaders, locale, maintenance, tenant, idempotency, featureFlags and auth are all written and unit-tested, through a chain each test builds by hand, and nothing else ever built one. A key now falls into one of three sets and every one of them means something. Nine are built and run in the order declared, wrapped around the handler so a refusal answers before the function runs and the headers the chain resolves reach a response that exists. One, csrf, is already enforced for every state-changing request whether or not it is declared, so declaring it is redundant rather than wrong. Two more are enforced by the generated request prelude rather than the chain, because they cannot be a middleware at all: the chain runs around the handler and by the time it has anything to say the body is in memory, so bodyLimit and uploadLimit are checked where the body is read -- the announced Content-Length first, without reading a byte, and then the read itself capped for a sender that announced nothing. Each shape gets its own number when both are declared, since a JSON body of several megabytes is a mistake and an upload of several megabytes is the feature. One wraps the handler and the chain both: tracing. The helper existed, was tested and was wired to nothing -- the key named it and the generator had never heard of either. It is outside the chain on purpose, because a request refused by a rate limit is still a request and a trace covering only the ones that got through is a latency graph with the slow half missing. csp sends the policy the project configured under dartvel.security.csp, and a route declaring the key with nothing configured fails the build: a policy is a statement about one application own scripts and origins, there is no default that could be right, and an empty header is not no policy -- a browser reads it as one that allows nothing. Five still fail the build as route middleware and each says why. policy belongs on the function annotation, which is the thing that carries a policy name. rateLimitCheckout and cacheTags have no code behind the name at all. cors and compression are answered for the whole server rather than per route -- CORS headers go on every response including the preflight, which never reaches a route -- and the reason they give now names a key somebody can set. It did not before: it said to pass cors: to the serve call, and nobody using Dartvel writes a serve call. The generated startBackend makes that call and read no configuration at all, so an application could not set a CORS policy and could not turn compression off. dartvel.server is read at generation time and emitted into it: the origins, methods, headers, exposed headers, credentials and preflight max-age of the policy, and whether responses are compressed. A caller passing either argument still overrides it; a generated entrypoint passes neither. Saying nothing means no CORS headers rather than answering every origin, because a server that answers every origin is the single setting most likely to be wrong and defaulting to it would put it on every application that never thought about the question. A value the build cannot honour stops the build rather than being ignored: credentials from origins: any, which a browser refuses itself so the policy would allow nothing; an origin written with a path or a trailing slash, which never matches the Origin header and reads as CORS being broken; and compression written as a string, which is not a boolean and would leave compression on for somebody who wrote down that they wanted it off. The example application configures a real policy, so the generated backend emits one and a compiler reads it. The middleware library was also not exported from the barrel, so an application could not import CommonMiddleware or MiddlewareChain without reaching into src. The page half was the same bug one scope over, and the specification opens this section with the page form. The router generator had never heard of the annotation. Its only reader anywhere was that backend spelling check, which walks every file under lib and therefore did validate a page key -- against the sets written for an HTTP chain -- so a page could declare auth and open for everybody, or declare bodyLimit and cap nothing, with a green build and a whitelisted name behind it. A page scope now answers for every key on its own terms, because nine of the backend keys cannot mean anything on a route activation: there is no Content-Length to read before a body arrives, no response whose headers a route could set, and no second party to rate limit, since the page and the visitor are one machine. Two run. A page middleware lives inside the router redirect, which returns a location or lets the route through, so auth and maintenance are the decisions of that shape, and both are emitted into the route in the order declared, ahead of the folder guards and the page own policy. That is the backend order, where the chain wraps the policy gate. Nothing replaces anything, because a page that picks up middleware and silently loses the folder guard it was moved behind is the failure this shape invites. A page guarded only by declared middleware also joins the guarded route list the sitemap writer reads, so a checkout page behind auth is no longer published to crawlers while the specification says authenticated routes are excluded by default. The two defaults point opposite ways on purpose. auth with nothing wired refuses, which is what DVPagePolicy already answers for a policy nobody can evaluate. maintenance with nothing wired reports the application up, because nobody wires that hook until they have a window to declare and reading silence as down would black out every application on the release that added it. Both redirect targets are exempt from their own check, since a sign-in page declaring auth would otherwise redirect to itself until go_router gives up with an exception naming the router rather than the page anybody would go looking at. And the router that carries the auth key carries the answer as well, reading DV.Auth, because a hook nothing sets is the same bug again: the guard would have refused the people who had just signed in, which is not the safe version of a guard but a feature nobody can use. The other seventeen keys fail the build with somewhere to put the thing instead -- bodyLimit at the backend function where the body is read, policy at the DVPage policy argument that carries a name, cors and compression at the server settings that answer for every response. The scope is the declaration rather than the file or the folder, because a file can hold a page and a backend function and one answer per file would refuse whichever came second, while a page can sit outside the pages directory and deciding by folder would let one annotation mean two things depending on where somebody dropped it. Absent on pages: the other three things the specification says page middleware can do. It can redirect and it can block; it cannot preload data, set SEO context, or defer a route bundle, because a redirect returns a location or nothing and has nowhere to leave a value the page would then read. Absent too are the layout, model and storage scopes the specification lists beside pages and backend functions. A DVUseMiddleware on a layout file now stops the build rather than wrapping nothing, which is the honest half of not having the scope: a _layout.dart declaring auth used to have its spelling checked and guard none of the pages under it, so a whole section looked protected in the source and was open in the build. On a model or a storage declaration the annotation is still read by nothing and still measured against the backend sets, because the scope test answers page or not-page. Each needs a scope of its own before its keys can be judged, and the layout one also needs a rule for how a layout key composes with the pages under it -- once for the subtree, or again per page -- which is a decision rather than a missing function. Global middleware has no configuration key at all: nothing under dartvel reads a list of keys to apply to everything. Maintenance has no configured source on the client either, so DVPageMiddleware.isDown is an extension point an application sets rather than something a build reads out of pubspec.yaml, and a maintenance window is code. DVPagePolicy.decide is likewise still set by nothing, which leaves a page policy default-deny until an application wires it; that belongs to the authorization section but sits in the same redirect, so it is named here rather than discovered there. Absent: what the five refused backend keys would do. policy belongs on the function annotation, which is the thing that carries a policy name, so a route middleware form of it would be a second place to say the same thing. rateLimitCheckout and cacheTags have no code behind the name at all, and each is a guess at a different feature -- one names a bucket an application would have to define, the other a set of tags a response would have to carry. cors and compression, if a per-route form is ever wanted, need a rule for how each composes with the server-wide setting -- whether a route's origins replace the server's or add to them, and what a route that turns compression on means inside a server that turned it off -- which is the reason those keys are refused rather than quietly accepted.
Biometric sign-in, which is a device capability rather than a server one and is tracked under Platform bindings. LDAP, SAML, passkey and Web3 ship.

binding_names.dart declares 87 names and no platform binds them all, which is the design rather than a gap: a tray is not a thing a browser has, and a resizable window is not a thing an Android application owns. What each target binds is its own capability set, and that set is now checked against the registrations rather than trusted -- android_bindings_test asserts the two agree by reading the source, and the emulator job asserts it again on a device, where a claim with no handler behind it looks exactly like a platform that cannot. Bound today: Linux 63, Windows 41, web 41, Android 36, macOS 36, iOS 7. Android moved from 10 to 36 and web from 16 to 41. Those figures date the moment they were written; dart tool/binding_coverage.dart counts them from the source, and prose here should be read against it rather than trusted. Absent on Android, each with the reason rather than a date: biometrics.authenticate, because BiometricPrompt reports to an AuthenticationCallback, which is an abstract class, and jnigen implements interfaces and cannot subclass one, so the prompt answer has nowhere to arrive until a Java shim is written beside the Context provider; nfc.readTag and nfc.writeTag, because a tag reaches an application only through foreground dispatch or reader mode, both Activity callbacks that fire whenever somebody taps, so a one-shot binding would answer null for ever or hand back whatever was tapped last; bluetooth.connect, disconnect and forget, because Android has no device-level connect at all, connection being per profile and asynchronous, and removeBond is hidden and blocked for ordinary applications; and display.enterFullscreen and exitFullscreen, which must run on Android main thread through Activity.runOnUiThread and so need java.lang.Runnable generated as an implementable interface, which needs an Android SDK to generate from. display.enableKiosk and disableKiosk stay unregistered on purpose, since DVDisplayControls falls back to kiosk.enforce and kiosk.release, which Android binds, and a second registration would be two answers to one question. On web the 44 unbound names each carry a written reason in dvWebUnavailableBindings and a test fails until a newly declared name joins one list or the other, so silence is not available: a tab has no tray, no global shortcut, no watchdog that outlives the event loop it runs on, and no path for a file somebody picked. Nine more are registered only where the browser has the API -- share.text, contacts and the NFC and Bluetooth names are absent from desktop Chrome, detected for rather than assumed -- and a refusal is told apart from an absence, DVWebPermissionDenied carrying the browser own words when somebody taps Deny where a missing API leaves the name unregistered. What has been run is narrower than what is implemented. On web, 32 of the 41 were exercised in headless Chrome, including an OPFS byte round trip and a real 11,315-byte PNG from a fake camera device; the rest need a tap, a modal or an Android Chrome, and Firefox and Safari are reasoned from their APIs rather than measured. On Android nothing below the Dart decision layer has been executed at all, because there is no device or emulator on the development machine, so every JNI call is implemented and unverified until the emulator job runs it. Two contracts disagree across platforms and both are live faults rather than gaps: notifications.sendLocal answers with the freedesktop notification id on Linux and a bool everywhere else while DVNotifications.sendLocalNotification requires a bool, so that call throws on Linux; and files.writeBytes returns a byte count from the shared native binding while DVFiles.writeBytes requires a bool, so it throws on Linux, Windows and macOS where web returns true and works. Sensors are the one place the declared surface is itself wrong: SensorManager has no read-now call and the declared name is singular, so Android binds a genuine one-shot while DVSensors types itself as a Stream that yields exactly once, and a real subscription would need a second name or a stream-shaped bridge.

Migrations run now, and did not: dartvel db migrate discovered a list of table names, printed a line per model saying it had migrated it and a total saying they were synced successfully, wrote a JSON snapshot, and executed nothing. The generated createTableSql -- one per model, correct, carrying the tenant column -- was called by nothing anywhere in the repository. The generator now writes the statements where something other than Dart can read them, built from the same column list the model itself carries, and the command runs them: SQLite because that is the one the framework can reach, through the framework own adapter rather than a second way to open the same file. Any other provider gets the statements written out with the reason they were not run, because the CLI has no connection to a managed Postgres and saying so is worth more than the green line it replaces. A table that already exists gains the columns its model gained, since CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS is a no-op against one that is there and a query naming a column the table lacks fails against a database just reported as migrated. The tenant column is the one that cannot be added quietly: rows written before it existed belong to no tenant, a predicate on every read hides all of them from everybody, and the table reads as empty in a way that cannot be told from data loss -- so such a table is left entirely alone, not half migrated, and the command asks whose the rows are. Absent: nothing. SQLite, PostgreSQL and MySQL, each with their wire-compatible variants, and TLS on both network engines so managed endpoints are reachable. MongoDB, ClickHouse and BigQuery are out of scope by decision, not backlog. Also absent: applying a migration to Postgres or MySQL from the CLI, which needs a connection it does not have; dropping or altering a column, since every generated column is TEXT and nothing has yet needed to change one; and a module tables, which are named at run time by how the module was mounted and are recorded by the parent own generation.

Built since: Dartvel reads an OpenAPI document as well as writing one. `dartvel import openapi <file|url>` turns a specification into ordinary source -- a private @DVModel per schema under lib/models/, a function per operation under lib/api/ with path parameters interpolated -- which is the direction people actually start from: an API exists, somebody hands you its spec, and the work is transcribing it by hand. A field the specification does not list in `required` is nullable, which is the difference between a model that matches the API and one that throws the first time a field is absent. A schema the importer cannot map is reported and skipped rather than emitted as `dynamic`: a guess that compiles is found at run time, and a line of output naming the schema is found now. Files already on disk are left alone unless --overwrite is passed, because an import that silently replaced an edited file is an import that gets run once. A Postman collection reads in too, because an OpenAPI document is the tidy case and what people are handed is very often somebody's export of the requests their team already makes. Requests become functions, folders are walked through, `:id` becomes a parameter that reaches the path, and Postman's {{baseUrl}} does not survive: the generated client knows where the API is, and left in it produces a request to a literal "{{baseUrl}}/books" that fails at run time and reads as a network problem. A collection carries no types, which is said once rather than discovered by looking in lib/models and finding nothing. Both importers share the writing half of the command and the naming rules -- two copies of the overwrite rule would be two chances to destroy somebody's edited file.

sections.absent: Absent: DVModelChangeKind.restored, which nothing publishes. A watcher handling it will never see that branch taken, because nothing in the framework restores a deleted model -- there is no soft delete to restore from. Named rather than published on some change that merely resembles one.

no provider has been exercised against a real APNS or push service. The SMTP provider is exercised against a real SMTP server now, in a container, with the raw source of what arrived read back -- which is the only way to see the half of this that is accepted and wrong, and it found two. The subject went down the wire as raw UTF-8 in a header RFC 5322 says is ASCII: the server took it, the companion assertion that it was still readable at the far end passed because that server guesses the encoding, and the clients that do not guess show it as mojibake to whoever was sent it. Headers are RFC 2047 encoded words now, split on character boundaries rather than on bytes, since a word broken mid-character decodes to a replacement in half the readers and leaves the subject wrong in exactly two places; an address keeps its angle brackets and only the display name is encoded, because encoding the whole thing produces a header no server can route. The body declared no transfer encoding at all, which means 7bit, which raw UTF-8 is not -- a server without 8BITMIME may refuse it or strip the high bit and the message arrives readable-ish, which is the worst outcome to be handed. Each part says what it is now: 7bit where the content really is, quoted-printable where it is not, which also keeps every line under the 998 octets RFC 5321 allows. Dot-stuffing, the AUTH exchange, multipart and the ordinary path were already right and are now proven against a server rather than against a connection this repository wrote. The native transport they depend on speaks HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 and is verified live, and the VAPID signature is pinned byte-for-byte to RFC 6979's published P-256 vectors rather than only round-tripped through this library's own verifier -- but a signature a push service would accept is not the same as a request one has accepted. Channel routing is built: DVNotificationMessage.channels used to be read by nothing, so the specification's own three-channel example delivered to the in-app provider and reported success; each channel now picks its own provider and resolves the recipient id to the address that provider needs through DVNotificationRoutes, push tries the native providers and falls back to Web Push both when none is registered and when the registered one fails, quiet hours hold only push, web push and SMS because holding an email drops it, and send returns a per-channel DVNotificationDelivery so a notification that was withheld and one that was lost are different answers. Mail priority reaches the wire as X-Priority and Importance instead of being dropped by all six providers, and SES no longer drops custom headers or recipient display names. Absent for want of work rather than credentials or hardware: delivery receipts and bounce or complaint webhooks as typed backend functions; attachments and tags on DVMailMessage, which the specification lists and the type does not carry; per-tenant sender identities and DKIM or SPF validation checks; List-Unsubscribe headers, so unsubscribe is a preference this framework honours internally and not one a mail client can act on; queued-by-default mail, which still sends inline although DV.Jobs and DV.Queues exist to carry it; a durable inbox and database notifications, since the in-app channel writes to whichever provider is registered and the only one shipped keeps a list in memory; server-side device token storage, rotation and revocation -- the device half of registration is reachable now that PushNotifications is exported at all, but where a token is kept between the device handing it over and a send needing it is still the application's problem, since DVNotificationRoutes only asks for it; per-channel rate limits; tenant-aware branding; and the pubspec notification permissions the specification says are validated at build time, for which no CLI or generator code reads a key -- the declaration does not exist at all, so there is nothing yet being parsed and dropped. The windows, macos, linux, tizen and webos provider kinds are enum members with no implementation behind them; routing will select one the moment it is registered, and until then a push on those platforms falls through to Web Push

Tenant resolution is built: DVTenants resolves the current tenant from the configured source, the tenant middleware makes it current for the rest of the chain, presence is scoped by it, and the tenant is held in a zone so it follows async work rather than leaking between concurrent requests. Filtering of generated model queries is built now and was not: the word tenant appeared zero times in the model generator and nowhere in any database adapter, so on the shared-database strategy the specification lists first, a query returned every tenant rows. A model that declares tenantScoped: true gets a dv_tenant column in its schema, a predicate on every read, the current tenant bound into every write, and a delete that cannot reach another tenant row. The schema, the writes and the reads arrive together on purpose -- a column written and not filtered on leaks, one filtered on and not written hides every row, and both look exactly like the feature working. It is opt-in per model because a single-tenant application should not carry a column it never reads and a table deliberately shared across tenants would be broken by a predicate it never asked for, and a model that declares a field of that name is refused at generation time rather than producing a duplicate column when the table is created in a deployment. A model that sets tenantScoped: true and generatePublicPages: true together is refused at generation time: a public page is rendered with no request, so there is no current tenant to scope it by, and the row would be served at a public URL to anybody -- the exact leak the column exists to close, on the one path that never sees it. Which model is scoped is read from that model own arguments now, and was read from the whole file: one tenant-scoped model made every model declared beside it tenant-scoped. The comment two lines above the read names the case it breaks -- a currency list, a country table -- and the symptom is not a leak but the opposite. Rows written before the column existed belong to no tenant, so a predicate the model author never asked for hides every one of them from every tenant. Schema-per-tenant and database-per-tenant do something now, and did not: both were an enum value and a name-building function -- DVTenants.qualifierFor, correct, unit tested, and called by nothing anywhere -- so configuring either produced exactly the queries sharedDatabase produces against exactly the same database. Every tenant read every tenant rows on the two strategies chosen specifically to prevent that, and it looked like it worked: every query returned rows and the application behaved. schemaPerTenant qualifies the name, resolved at the moment a statement runs rather than written in, because which schema is asking is a fact about the request and two requests are in flight at once; under sharedDatabase the same call returns the table own name, so the strategy almost everyone uses generates what it always did. databasePerTenant does not qualify the name, since the connection is what differs and a qualified one would look for a schema inside the tenant own database; the adapter is resolved per tenant instead, opened once each and kept, because a connection per query is a pool nobody wrote and on SQLite a second write lock over one file. Configuring that strategy without saying how to open a tenant database is refused, the fallback being the one adapter for everybody -- the leak it exists to close, returning rows the whole time. A migration for an existing table is built too: a table with rows gaining the tenant column is left entirely alone until somebody says whose those rows are, because rows written before the column existed belong to nobody and a predicate on every read hides all of them, so the table reads as empty in a way nothing distinguishes from data loss. A raw query an application writes itself is checked now, and was not: generated model queries carried the predicate and everything else did not -- a report, a dashboard count, a join the generator cannot express, a query written before the model was scoped -- each of which returned rows that looked plausible while showing one tenant another tenant data. The generated client registers which tables are scoped, because the database layer has no idea what a model is, and a statement naming one without mentioning the column is refused. Deliberately coarse: a false positive is a refusal somebody reads and fixes, a false negative leaves the old behaviour, and the one thing it never does is guess in the direction of allowing. Writes are checked as well, the worse half, since a write without the column puts a row in the table belonging to nobody that every tenant then cannot see. Names match on a word boundary, so workorders is not orders -- refusing it would teach people to reach for the escape hatch out of habit, which is how an escape hatch stops meaning anything. Only under sharedDatabase, the other two separating by schema or connection where a predicate on a column that is not there would fail every query. Registration adds rather than replaces, since an application client and every module client run in one process and replacing would leave whichever ran last as the only checked set. DV.Database.acrossTenants is the way through, for an operator report or a support tool: not hard, but written down, visible in a diff and greppable rather than a query that happened to have no predicate. The tenant a request named is held for that request now, and was written to a process-wide field. A server has more than one request in flight and Dart hands the isolate over at every await, so the request that arrived second decided what the first one read: every query the first handler made after its next await ran as somebody else's tenant, returned rows, and rendered. withTenant existed, carried the tenant in a zone, was unit tested, and was called by nothing on the request path. Every generated route is wrapped now rather than only the routes that listed the tenant middleware, because a tenant-scoped model does not care what the route declared -- and the plainest raw handlers had a shortcut registration with no wrapper on them at all. The middleware still makes the tenant current for a hand-written server that runs the chain itself, and stops writing the process-wide field when a scope already carries it, since under a scope that write belongs to no request and reaches every one of them. A request naming no tenant keeps what the process was set to, so a single-tenant deployment on an apex domain is not pushed onto a default tenant with no rows in it. Server rendering resolved no tenant at all, and kept each page under the request path alone. Both halves are one hole and either fixed alone would have looked like a fix and been none: a tenant in the key with nothing resolving one is always the same tenant, and a resolved tenant with a shared key still serves the first arrival page. Under the subdomain source the specification lists first, acme.example.com/orders and globex.example.com/orders are one path, so the first tenant to ask filled the entry and every other tenant read that page until the ttl ran out -- no login and no crafted request, two customers on one server was enough. The preview and web-server handler had the same two faults, which matters because that target exists to promise that the page a developer previews is the page the server sends. An export declared a tenant and narrowed by nothing. DVExportOptions.tenantId was stored, written into the file metadata, and read by nothing that chose which rows were written, while policyFilter beside it in the same object did narrow -- one filter and one label, reading as two filters, and a file that names a tenant it was never narrowed to is worse than one that names none because somebody downstream reads the label. It cannot be narrowed there: the rows were read before the export was called and the tenant column is not a field on the generated model, so there is nothing on an item to compare. A declared tenant that is not the tenant the export runs as is refused, with the order that works, rather than stamped. Full-text search over a scoped table returned every tenant rows. The Postgres provider builds its own SQL and hands it to the adapter, so it went past DV.Database and past the check that refuses a statement naming a scoped table without the tenant column, and the automatic tenant filter the specification names was a hook called filter that every application had to write for itself: one that did not got a search box listing other tenants rows, with their titles and descriptions in the results, because that is what search results are. The predicate is added before the application own filter, so a filter that throws or is written wrong cannot be the reason it is missing. Under a schema per tenant the name is qualified instead and no column predicate is added, and the index is created on the tenant own table rather than in whichever schema the connection points at. Choosing an isolation strategy is possible from a project at all now. It meant calling DVTenants.configure from Dart that no generated entrypoint runs, so schema-per-tenant and database-per-tenant -- the two an application picks precisely to keep tenants in separate schemas or separate databases -- could not be selected, and every deployment ran the shared-database default whether that is what it wanted or not. requireTenant was in the same position: it gated the refusal of a request naming no tenant and nothing anywhere set it. dartvel.tenancy is read at generation time and emitted where the server starts, and a value nobody implements fails the build rather than being dropped, because a misspelled isolation left on the floor runs the default while the pubspec says otherwise and every query still returns rows. Absent: creating the per-tenant schemas and databases themselves, which needs a list of tenants the build does not have. And the tenant does not travel with a job. DVJobEnvelope has no tenant field and no queue adapter persists one, so work dispatched during one tenant request runs later as whatever the worker process is set to -- writing rows that belong to nobody, or reading another tenant. That is implementable and unbuilt rather than blocked: it wants a column on the durable jobs table with a migration for tables that predate it, the same field in the five broker encodings, and the worker running each handler inside the envelope tenant. Carrying it on some queues and dropping it on others would leave work looking tenant-aware while the durable path lost it, which is the failure this section keeps finding, so it is named here whole rather than started. Hosted search is unscoped too: Meilisearch and OpenSearch answer from documents the application shapes, so the tenant has to be a field in the index and a filter on the query rather than something a provider can add to somebody else's schema.

Guarded routes are excluded from sitemap.xml now, and were not until this was written: the sitemap was built by scraping every path: literal out of the generated router with a regular expression, which cannot see the redirect guard block below the path it just matched, so /admin and everything behind a folder guard was published to crawlers. The specification says private routes are excluded by default and it was not true. The generator now writes dartvelGuardedRoutes into router.g.dart and the build reads it. Per-route sitemap tuning is built now, and was not: dartvel.seo.sitemap.enabled, .exclude and .defaults were documented and parsed nowhere, and DVPageSitemap and DVSitemapChangeFrequency appeared in the specification example and in no Dart file, so every route was written out as a <loc> and nothing else. A page tunes its own entry through the annotation and the project sets the rest, a page overriding the defaults field by field so that saying only that it changes daily keeps the project priority. A route neither mentions stays a bare URL: a priority nobody asked for says the same thing as none, in more bytes, and a crawler cannot tell it was invented. A priority outside 0 to 1 and a changefreq outside the seven words sitemaps.org defines are refused rather than clamped or dropped, because a crawler discards the whole url element when a child will not validate. exclude patterns take the section index with the section, since publishing the front door of a hidden area discloses what the pattern was written to hide, and enabled: false stops robots.txt naming a file the build did not write. Adding the argument found a worse thing than the gap it filled: it is a call, and every parser of the page annotation here was written to stop at the first close parenthesis, so a page carrying it was not discovered at all -- no route in the router, no node in the project graph, on a build that succeeded -- and a policy written after it fell outside the captured text and was not read, which generates a page that declared a guard open to everybody. Parentheses are counted now, string literals and comments excluded, and the example application declares the annotation so the real generator reads it and a compiler reads what it emitted. A module mount carrying sitemap: exclude is left out now, and was not: the key was parsed, reached the mount and was written into the generated route index, and the sitemap writer never asked -- so every route of a module mounted to stay out went into the parent sitemap.xml anyway. The same failure as the guarded routes above, in the one place a comment said it was handled. The routes are still answered and still redirected to, because the exclusion is about being advertised rather than reachable and dropping the redirect would break a link somebody already has, so the sitemap and the web server manifest ask different functions. Also absent from the guarded list: module mount routes, which carry that key instead, and generated model public pages, which are public by annotation.

Nothing this section lists is unbuilt. Background sync is exercised in a real browser: the generated worker keeps an IndexedDB outbox of same-origin non-GET requests that could not be sent, answers the caller with a 202 and X-Dartvel-Queued, and replays the outbox in order when the network is back, stopping at the first failure and one replay at a time (a sync event and the client's replay message arriving together sent everything twice until they shared one in-flight promise). dartvel capture pwa-sync loads the built worker in Chrome, takes the server away, makes a POST, brings the server back and expects the POST to arrive; the Runtime verification workflow runs it against the site's own build on every push, and it is what found the double replay. Everything else the section lists is built: manifest, viewport, service worker, offline page, install prompt, and icon generation from web/icon.png through the CLI own PNG codec. The install prompt had two defects in one path until they were found by asking which enum values nothing produces. DVInstallOutcome.dismissed was produced by nothing: show returned a static that only a test seam ever set, so a browser reported accepted whatever the person at the screen chose, and then marked the application installed -- which hides the affordance, so an application somebody declined could never be installed from inside it again. And the binding that calls the browser own prompt was written and called by nothing, so tapping Install opened no dialog at all: the feature flipped two flags and returned. The outcome comes from the browser now, through the bridge like every other platform call, and the binding waits for it, since prompt only opens the dialog and the choice arrives on userChoice afterwards. Anything other than the word accepted is a dismissal, because treating an unrecognised third answer as acceptance would install nothing and say it had. The tests that existed set the outcome themselves and asserted it came back, which proves the seam rather than the path, and is why this survived

Shorebird-backed native patch application; page bundles ship as data and do not need it. check() joins every rule into one decision -- the channel's offer, this device's place in the staged rollout, a version the application pinned, a version somebody skipped, and a kiosk's maintenance window -- so they cannot disagree and none of them is enforced nowhere. What that decision is made about has no source, though, and that is the larger gap. updates.check, updates.apply and updates.rollback are declared binding names that nothing registers on any platform; DVUpdates.check reaches updates.check through DVNativeBridge.require, which throws when nothing is registered, and the only registrations anywhere are the stubs three test files install. So the rules are right, well tested, and unreachable: DV.Updates.check() throws in every real application on every target until something binds those three names to an update source. Found by dart tool/binding_coverage.dart, which counts registrations from the source instead of reading a claim written here.

@DVAITool is generated and registered now. It was generated only: the list carried a name, a description, an import URI and a file path, and nothing anywhere turned one into something callable -- an assistant could read that a function existed and had no way to run it. The generated file now emits a JSON Schema per tool, because every provider requires one on each tool, and a handler that reads the arguments out of the input object and calls the function; the generated backend registers them before it serves. An argument of the wrong type is refused by name rather than coerced, since a tool that quietly received 0 for a number it could not read would run and be wrong, which is what a schema exists to prevent. Absent: a tool returning a type DVJsonCodec cannot represent throws when the result is encoded rather than being converted, because guessing at a model class serialization would produce a shape no provider was told about; and the schema advertises a type per parameter and nothing else -- no descriptions, enums or required-field list beyond nullability.

Logs, profiling, performance analysis, error reporting, structured diagnostics with fix-recommendations, structured AI-readable logs, and the DV.log / DV.ObservabilityAndLogging.event API the spec names are all unbuilt -- there is no log sink anywhere in the runtime, so nothing an application logs goes anywhere. What is real: DVMetrics renders Prometheus text exposition and GET /metrics serves it, DVHealth backs GET /health with real checks on a deadline, and tracing carries W3C Trace Context across the request boundary with sampling decided from the trace id alone -- a per-process decision samples a four-service request with probability p^4, which reads as tracing being on and finding nothing. Spans are captured into an in-process ring buffer, served at /_dartvel/traces when diagnostics endpoints are on and nowhere else: there is no OTLP exporter, so no span reaches a collector. Distributed Tracing has the full account. dartvel logs, dartvel traces and dartvel metrics used to paper over this with hardcoded sample output; dartvel metrics now fetches the real GET /metrics endpoint and reports plainly when no server answers or nothing has been recorded, and dartvel logs / dartvel traces now say outright that they have nothing to read instead of inventing a trace id or a log line

Nothing reaches a collector: the exporter interface exists with in-memory, ring-buffer and fanout implementations, and there is no OTLP exporter, so spans leave the process only through /_dartvel/traces when diagnostics endpoints are on. The only span most requests have is the request itself -- dvTraced is the sole place that starts one, so there are no spans for database queries, outbound HTTP, queue publish and consume, transactions or AI calls. Trace context does not travel in the job envelope, so nothing links a job back to the request that enqueued it. There are no client spans and no ingest for them. Span attribute limits and the maximum span duration are unimplemented. dartvel traces reads nothing but the local buffer. The DV-TRACE codes are registered meanings and nothing emits one yet. What is real: W3C traceparent parsing and serialization, spans with attributes, errors and status, a sampler that decides from the trace id so every service in a trace agrees without coordinating, the HTTP middleware that joins or starts a trace and returns the traceparent on the response, and the trace id on every log line.

Nothing named. Generated factories now carry a sequence, so two create() calls produce two records rather than one repeated identifier, with createMany for list-shaped tests and resetSequence so a snapshot assertion is repeatable. Every test mode resolves, and a mode with no tests reports that it has none and where it looked

Algolia is exercised only against a recorded transport: it is a hosted service with no local server, so its request shape is pinned by unit tests rather than by a round trip. Meilisearch and OpenSearch are verified live in CI.

App-store and Play Billing purchases, which need the store bindings and a device to run them against. Stripe and Paddle are built: checkout for a plan, webhooks that grant and revoke entitlements from subscription status, trials, and usage meters. Each webhook is believed only when its own signature scheme matches in constant time within five minutes (Stripe's t=/v1= over 't.payload', Paddle's ts=/h1= over 'ts:payload', and each provider refuses the other's), with the key never echoed in an error and a sandbox Paddle key routed to the sandbox host by the key itself. Nothing here has been exercised against either service; the tests inject the HTTP and the clock. Four things were declared and read by nothing, which is this section's whole history. BillingPlan.priceMinorUnits and BillingPlan.currency were required constructor arguments no provider looked at: both took prices[plan.id] and sent the customer to whatever that identifier costs, so the example's pricing page could render 40.00 while the checkout charged 49.00 after a dashboard edit, and no code was in a position to notice. Checkout now reads the price from the provider first and refuses on any difference in amount or currency, before a session exists rather than after, so a mismatch leaves no orphan checkout that could still be handed to somebody; a tiered Stripe price reports no unit amount and is refused rather than skipped, since treating nothing-to-compare as agreement waves through the exact case. Reading a price needs a GET, so the fetch typedef became DVBillingFetch and carries the method. Trials were in the feature list and on nothing: Stripe takes the plan's trialDays with the session, and only when there is one, because a zero would silently cancel a trial configured on the price; Paddle keeps trials on the price and so checks both directions, since a promised fortnight the price does not give produces a support ticket while a trial nobody declared gives a week away per signup and produces nothing. Usage-based billing existed as two words in the specification. DVUsageMeter names what an application counts, the provider's event name is provider configuration, and recording against an unconfigured meter is an error rather than a no-op -- usage counted by the application and billed by nobody is the failure worth the check. The idempotency key is required because Dartvel's own queues redeliver and a provider counts one meter event per identifier, so a generated default would differ on the retry and double a bill. And the customer key: every provider stored grants under customer.toString(), which for an ordinary Dart object is the constant Instance of 'User', so passing the logged-in user -- what a parameter typed Object invites -- filed every user under one key and one subscription unlocked the plan for everybody, with no symptom except revenue that never arrived. An identity is now required, stated by DVBillingCustomer or by a String, a number or a meaningful toString, and the default toString is an ArgumentError naming the type. One behaviour bug went with them: both providers applied webhooks in arrival order, and Stripe does not guarantee one while a retried Paddle notification lands behind whatever was sent while it was failing, so a stale active behind a cancellation handed a cancelled customer their entitlement back -- signed, genuine, answered with a 200. Each provider now tracks the newest applied event per subscription, strictly older is stale and still acknowledged, and DVBillingWebhookResult.stale says why nothing changed. Invoices list now, through DV.Billing and both providers, with the amount as a DVMoney rather than an integer -- 4000 without its currency renders as forty dollars, four thousand yen or forty of whatever the page assumed -- and a status nothing recognises maps to unknown rather than to paid, since an unpaid invoice shown as settled is a bill nobody chases. A row that comes back for another customer is dropped: the query filters at the provider, so one that does not means the filter did not apply, and rendering it shows somebody another person's billing history on a page that looks entirely normal. Still absent: Usage reporting to Paddle, which bills metered items by adjusting subscription item quantities rather than through anything meter-shaped; it throws rather than accepting a record it would drop. Entitlements live in provider memory, so a restart loses every grant a webhook made and a second process cannot see them -- it fails closed, denying access rather than giving it, but a paying customer is denied until the next webhook. The webhook endpoint is not generated. Verification is reachable now -- DVBillingWebhookReceiver names the contract, each provider says which header it signs under, and DV.Billing.handleWebhook takes the request headers and finds it whatever case they arrive in, so a route no longer has to downcast or write the HMAC comparison itself, which is the version that gets simplified until an unsigned subscription activated is accepted. What is still missing is the route: the application declares the path and hands the payload over, so the specification's generated backend function with signature validation is a facade method a handler calls, not something the generator emits. Entitlement checks are not wired into policies or into any generated UI guard. Conversion rates are set by the application and no provider supplies them, and localisation does not yet choose a display currency on its own.

Nothing this section asks for is unbuilt. Switch control and hardware-key navigation are built: DVSwitchControl steps focus through a page with one key and activates with another, wrapping, with auto-scan for a single-switch user; DVHardwareKeys maps a remote's D-pad and select onto focus and activation; DVAccessibilityToggle is the attract-route toggle behind DV.Accessibility.switchControl; DVAccessibilityKeys.isExempt names the keys a kiosk hardware-key block must let through, which is the rule Kiosk Mode's native enforcement consults when it exists (that enforcement is Kiosk Mode's gap, not this section's). Waivers are built: dartvel.accessibility.waivers names a route, a rule the audit has (or * for the page) and a reason -- no reason, no waiver -- and a waiver that matches nothing is reported so it does not sit in the file for ever. The release gate is built: dartvel build web audits the semantics tree a real browser produced -- what a screen reader is actually handed -- and fails on a link or control with no accessible name, an empty heading, a page with no headings or no level 1, and a heading level skipped going down; on its first run against the site it found /features going h1 to h3. Generated tables have keyboard navigation, focus that survives a sort, and per-cell announcements naming the column and the row position. Contrast is checked against WCAG ratios and tap targets against Material's minimum

Drag and drop is built: a window accepts drops of the kinds it says it takes -- files, text, or both -- and each drop arrives as what was dropped and where, an empty drop or one after stop reaching nobody; on Linux the toplevel becomes a GTK drop target whose drag-data-received payload is read by its type, so one path serves a file manager's uri-list and a browser's text, and what GTK already took is kept and given back on stop. The uri-list is parsed as RFC 2483 has it, percent escapes decoded and a URI that is not a file left out. Exercised under Xvfb against real GTK, with a real GtkSelectionData built through the clipboard and the signal emitted the way a drop emits it. The tray is built on Linux, as the protocol has it rather than as a picture: a StatusNotifierItem and its com.canonical.dbusmenu menu are exported on the session bus and registered with the shell's StatusNotifierWatcher, which is how a modern desktop is told about a tray icon -- no XEmbed, nothing deprecated, no GTK. The suite stands up a watcher of its own the way a shell would, reads the item's title, icon, status, category and menu path back over the bus, walks the menu layout, sends an Event the way a click arrives and sees it reach the application by id, and watches the name leave the bus on hide. What a runner cannot check is the pixels, and nothing claims them: a desktop with no watcher leaves the item exported and says so. Drag and drop is built on all three desktops. On Windows it is an OLE drop target: a COM object with a vtable of seven functions, registered with RegisterDragDrop, reading CF_HDROP for the files a file manager drags and CF_UNICODETEXT for a browser's text, with the POINTL each method takes declared as the eight bytes it travels in rather than as a struct by value in a callback; the live suite gives it a real IDataObject -- the clipboard's, which is the same interface Explorer hands over, carrying a DROPFILES built the way a file manager builds one -- and calls Drop the way OLE calls it. On macOS the window's content view is registered as a dragging destination and the two dragging methods are added to its class at runtime, reading the whole file list a file manager writes rather than the first of it; the live suite checks that reading against a real pasteboard, files and text, and that a process with no window is refused and says so. What a runner cannot do is drag from another application: on both, the drag is not claimed and everything the drop does is. The file associations register at run time on all three desktops, which is the half an installer normally does and which an application copied into place has nobody to do: DV.Platform.associations writes the user's own desktop entry, MIME package and default-applications list on Linux -- files, so it works on a kiosk with no desktop session -- the per-user half of the registry under HKCU\\Software\\Classes on Windows, and on macOS registers the running bundle with LaunchServices and claims the types its Info.plist declares. Per-user everywhere, because the machine-wide equivalents need administrator rights and an API that asked for them is one most applications could not call. The refusals are stated rather than swallowed: a macOS process with no bundle has nothing to register and says so, and macOS has no public call to stop being the default for a type, so unregistering hands it back to whoever held it before and says when it cannot. Registering nothing, or a type with no extensions, is refused where it is called -- every platform matches a file by its extension. The launch handover is now exercised on both, since the single-instance lock's two-process suite runs on those runners as well as on Linux. The device and fleet APIs are built on Linux: the capability manifest (a provisioned or generated-and-kept id; cores, memory, kernel, display, touch, and the bindings actually registered rather than the names declared), health as a verdict with uptime, load, memory, disk and temperature behind it from procfs and sysfs, a watchdog that restarts on a missed heartbeat and tells systemd through sd_notify so WatchdogSec= works, restart-loop detection reported as DV-KIOSK-008 instead of restarting again, provisioning kept across starts, and a diagnostics bundle. File associations and app links are built on Linux: dartvel build linux writes the desktop entry (Exec with %U, MimeType for every association and x-scheme-handler for every scheme) and shared-mime-info XML for the types the app introduces from dartvel.desktop in pubspec.yaml, and the generated runtime opens what the app was launched with -- DVAppLaunch takes the single-instance lock, maps each argument to a route without trusting it as one, opens it as an external window request, and a later launch hands its arguments to the first and ends. Printing is built on Linux: DV.Platform.Printing draws pictures onto pages through GtkPrintOperation, to a PDF with no dialog (verified under Xvfb, poppler reading the page count back) or through the print dialog. System dialogs are built on Linux: DV.Platform.Dialogs opens, saves, chooses a folder and shows a message through GTK, verified under Xvfb by a seam that answers the dialog from GTK's own loop the way a person would. Built on Linux and tested under Xvfb: global shortcuts, grabbed through XGrabKey on a pump isolate's own X connection with XTest pressing the keys in the test; and the application menu, built as a real GtkMenuBar into the toplevel window with the view reparented beneath it, read back through GTK and activated by id. Both have the Dart side everywhere -- DVAccelerator parsed once, DVShortcuts and DVMenus delivering by id. Built since on Windows and macOS, each exercised on its own runner by the live suite: global shortcuts (RegisterHotKey on a pump thread of its own that delivers WM_HOTKEY by id, proven by posting the message Win32 sends and by a synthesised press where the session takes input; Carbon's RegisterEventHotKey with one handler dispatching by id, registration and the refusal of a duplicate proven, delivery said to need the application's event loop); the application menu (a Win32 menu bar on the process's window, subclassed so WM_COMMAND is dispatched by id, proven on a window the test owns; NSMenu as NSApp's main menu with every item targeting one runtime-defined Objective-C object, read back and activated through AppKit); the tray icon with its menu delivered by id (Shell_NotifyIcon on the process's window, refused where the session has no notification area; an NSStatusBar item sharing the menu's target under a second action) -- the Dart side of the tray now delivers a chosen item to onSelected and the selected stream; and the device APIs, the shared runtime reading through Win32 and through sysctl, Mach and getloadavg, real numbers from each runner.
