Multi-window and window state persistence are recorded under Multi-Window Startup is measured: the framework marks the phases it goes through -- configure, the generated registrations, the platform bindings, and the first frame, measured after the frame because a router that is built is not a screen that is up -- from one monotonic clock, and the report is the same shape every run, so two runs of the same build are comparable line by line and a budget names the phase that went over. The running application publishes it beside its live window list and the diagnostics bundle carries it, so a fleet asking why a device is slow to come up has the answer without sending anybody to the device; CI reads it back from the Linux run. Boot-to-app packaging is built for the eLinux target: autostart, restartOnFailure and a declared watchdog become the systemd unit the bundle installs, and the generated unit is handed to systemd-analyze in CI, so a directive systemd would reject is found at build time rather than at boot. Update channels for kiosk and device fleets are built: DV.Updates.check and apply take a channel, a staged rollout decides from the device and the version so a device asked twice is answered the same and a device held back can say so, and kiosk.updates decides when a kiosk may apply what it found -- inside a maintenance window that may run past midnight, only with staff present, or immediately, with a required update resetting the session instead of waiting. The serial port is built on Linux: DV.Platform.device.serial lists the ports udev keeps stable names for, opens one in raw mode at a speed the kernel has a constant for, reads with a timeout that survives the signals a Dart VM raises, writes, and closes -- exercised against a real pseudo-terminal in CI, where the bytes, the termios speed and the timeout are checked on real file descriptors. The USB bus is read on Linux: DV.Platform.device.usb lists what is plugged in, out of sysfs, with each device's vendor and product ids as hex, what it says about itself, and where it sits on the bus -- interfaces are not counted as devices, a device with no readable id is not reported with a wrong one, and a bus that is not there is no devices rather than an error. Talking to a device is built now as well, through usbfs rather than libusb -- libusb is a dependency to ship, a licence to carry and a shared object to find on a device that may be read-only, and the interface underneath it is four ioctls. The care goes into those numbers, because they are computed rather than named: one packs a direction, the size of the struct it takes, a type letter and an index into thirty-two bits, and getting any of the four wrong still produces a valid ioctl, so the kernel runs a different call or answers ENOTTY and neither says which field was wrong. They come from one rule and are checked against what the kernel headers define, including the direction bits, where read is 2 and write is 1 -- the opposite of the order anybody says them in. What the errors mean is the other half, and on a device node none of them is general: a permission error is a udev rule nobody has written rather than a fault in the calling code, and somebody handed errno 13 goes and rereads their own transfer loop; a busy interface is a kernel driver already holding it, usbhid on anything that looks like a keyboard, which needs detaching and never yields to a retry; a stall is the device refusing the request rather than the transfer failing; and a timeout is a device that may answer next time, which a kiosk told otherwise stops asking. Callers hold a handle rather than a file descriptor, since a descriptor is shared with every other open file in the process. Closing releases every claimed interface first, because a descriptor closed with one still claimed leaves the kernel driver unbound until the device is replugged -- so the next run finds hardware that no longer works and nothing that says why. Bluetooth is read on Linux through BlueZ on the bus: DV.Platform.Bluetooth answers whether any adapter's radio is on, lists the adapters, and lists every device the machine knows about -- paired, connected or merely seen -- with the name it has given, its signal strength and the adapter that knows it. A device that has never said its name is still reported, because dropping it would tell a fleet a paired thing is not there; and a machine with no BlueZ running says so rather than answering with the empty list that means nothing is paired. Exercised in CI against a BlueZ of the suite's own on the session bus. Pairing, connecting and forgetting are built too, which is the half a fleet needs: a reader that has come unpaired in a lobby is otherwise a kiosk somebody has to drive to. Almost none of it is a plain call, because BlueZ's worst answers look like ordinary failures. Pairing something already paired is an error whose right answer is that the device is paired, since a caller told otherwise retries forever against a reader that works. Pair with no agent registered comes back as an authentication cancellation, which reads as a pairing problem and is not one -- there is nobody standing at a headless device to answer a passkey -- so it is said in those words rather than sending whoever reads it to check the radio, the range and the battery first. Connecting something unpaired is refused before the radio is used at all, so it says to pair first instead of leaving a timeout to be diagnosed. Disconnecting something already disconnected is the outcome that was asked for. And unpairing is the adapter's method rather than the device's, so the adapter the device says it is on is the one asked -- on a machine with two, asking the other removes nothing and answers success. A device is named by address, because that is what is on the label, and matched without regard to case, because BlueZ spells its own paths in upper case and a literal comparison reports no such device for one sitting on the desk. NFC is read on Linux through neard: DV.Platform.NFC answers whether there is a reader that could read something now -- a powered adapter, not merely a present one -- and what is written on the tag currently on it. No tag is null rather than an error, because that is the normal state of a reader nobody has tapped, while no neard at all says so: the difference between 'hold your card nearer' and 'this unit's reader is not running'. Exercised in CI against a neard of the suite's own. Writing a tag is built too, which is the half a kiosk needs to hand somebody a card -- a locker key, a visitor badge, a pallet label. Almost every way it goes wrong still looks like it worked, so almost none of it is a straight call: a URI is written as a URI record rather than as text that looks like one, because a link in a text record reads back as exactly those characters and does nothing when a phone touches it; the scheme is matched against a list rather than taken from anything with a colon in it, so a value like Type2:something stays text instead of becoming a URI no reader can follow; every text record carries a language code, which NDEF requires and some readers show an empty record without; an empty value is refused, since a tag written with nothing on it cannot be told from one never written; and a read-only tag is refused before the write with the reason, because somebody told only that it failed presents the same locked card again. What neard itself says when the chip refuses -- the tag was taken off the reader, the record did not fit -- is passed through rather than flattened. Exercised against the suite's own neard, which records the dictionary it was handed, so what actually reaches the tag is checked rather than that a call was made. Clipboard and selection integration was the one item on this section's own list that nothing had claimed, and it was worse than unclaimed. A copy reported success and put nothing on the clipboard any other application could read. On X11 a copy does not hand bytes to the server; it makes the process the owner of the CLIPBOARD selection, and every other application that wants the text asks this process and waits for an answer that comes out of the GLib main loop. A Dart process runs no such loop, so a Dartvel copy did not merely fail to share -- it took the clipboard away from the whole session, and every paste anywhere hung until the application asking gave up. Nothing caught it because GTK answers the owner out of its own cache: reading the value back inside the process that wrote it returns the text whether or not a byte ever left. It is checked from a second process now, with its own connection to the display, which is the only thing that can tell the difference, and a write starts a pump that drains the main context. Under a real Flutter run the embedder already owns that context on the platform thread and the pump does nothing, which is right, because there the embedder is already answering. The selection half came with it: the PRIMARY selection, where highlighted text goes and a middle click pastes it, separate from what Ctrl+C put on the clipboard, through DV.Platform.clipboard.readSelection and writeSelection. Linux only, and that is a fact about the other platforms rather than a hole -- Windows and macOS have one clipboard and nothing that answers a middle click, so they leave the binding unregistered and say so instead of aliasing it onto copy and quietly destroying whatever the user had copied. A kiosk that locks the clipboard locks the selection too, that being the other way text somebody else left behind gets into one. The refusals arrive as failed futures rather than synchronous throws, which paste got wrong: the signature says Future, so a caller writing paste().catchError(...) never saw the kiosk refusal and it left their frame. The serial port is built on macOS too, and not by copying: macOS's termios has eight-byte flag words where Linux has four, twenty control characters where Linux has thirty-two, and speeds that are the numbers themselves rather than small indices, so a structure carried across would read the wrong fields and set a speed nobody asked for on a port that looks like it is working. Ports are the /dev/cu.* doors rather than /dev/tty.*, because opening the tty door waits for a carrier a three-wire cable never asserts. Exercised against a pseudo-terminal on the macOS runner. The serial port is built on Windows too, which is the third desktop and the last one it was missing from. Ports come from HKLM\HARDWARE\DEVICEMAP\SERIALCOMM, the list Windows itself keeps and the one every serial library reads -- walking the setup device tree instead finds ports that exist and cannot be opened -- and the value under each key is the COM name a caller opens rather than the driver path it is filed under. The list is sorted by number and not as text, so COM10 comes after COM9 rather than before it, and a value that is not a COM name is left out, because that key carries virtual devices on some machines and handing one back produces an open that fails for a reason nobody asked about. Every port is opened through the device-namespace path, not only the ones above COM9: the prefix is legal for all of them, and a rule with an exception at nine is a bug waiting for somebody's tenth adapter. The port is opened exclusively, which is the only way Windows will open one, configured through a DCB with SetCommState and given read timeouts with SetCommTimeouts. An open that fails says which port and why in words -- not there, or held by another program, which are different problems with different fixes -- rather than a Win32 number somebody has to go and look up. The parts that can be wrong quietly are string work and are held to account on any host; CreateFileW itself runs on the Windows runner, where the case worth proving is a machine with no serial hardware at all: enumerating is an empty list rather than an error, and a port that is not there is refused by name. The device APIs come up without a desktop, which is the machine they were written for: the fleet APIs, the serial port, the USB bus, Bluetooth and NFC are registered before the desktop libraries are opened and whether or not they open, because an eLinux kiosk with DRM and no X server has all of them and none of them touches X11. A headless registration claims no clipboard, no window and no tray, because a binding that answers where there is nothing to answer with is worse than one that is absent. Three more options were declared, documented, and read by nothing, which is this section's recurring fault rather than three unrelated ones. A window that said it took files only still handed the application a URL dragged out of a browser: the GTK target list is a request to the desktop and not a guarantee, and the Linux handler read the type off whatever arrived and delivered it, while Windows and macOS had gated the same thing since they were written. The old test asserted the target list, which is the shape of the request; the new ones drop the wrong kind on a real window and check that nobody hears about it. File associations rewrote the desktop entry and the MIME package from nothing on every call, so a second register threw away the first call's types and unregistering one type deleted the entry for all of them -- while mimeapps.list stayed selective and went on naming this application as the handler, leaving the desktop sending files to an entry that was not on disk. Both merge now, and the files still go when the last type does. And a print job title crossed the bridge to Linux and was read by nobody, so the queue showed GTK's own "<program> job #1" while the caller had named the job; Windows had honoured the same option all along, which is what this fault looks like from the calling side -- an option that works on one desktop and does nothing on the next, with no way to tell them apart. What is still absent is inside the items rather than an item, and is worth naming rather than implying. Three declared options are honoured on fewer platforms than they are offered on: macOS registers a file type by its extension alone, so the mimeType and the description a caller declares reach nothing there; macOS flattens every open/save filter into one unlabelled list of extensions, so named filters do not become the chooser's popup they become on Linux and Windows; and Windows' folder chooser drops initialDirectory and opens wherever the shell decides. Each of those is on a runner this machine is not, so each is named from the code rather than measured. On Linux the pages a print reports are the pages that were sent: GTK draws only the pages a user picked in the dialog and DVPrintResult.pages still claims the lot, which is a wrong number that looks entirely plausible and has had no test effort at all. dialogs.message answers true on all three whatever the desktop did, and macOS's PDF export is US Letter by size wherever it runs. The clipboard carries text and only text on every target: an image or a fragment of HTML copied out of a Dartvel application is not on the clipboard at all.

The policy, the state machine and the enforcement matrix are built and validated by dartvel doctor, which fails a build configuration whose policy cannot be honoured. The session clock is built: the runtime notices idle, counts down for the warning span on a signal the countdown route reads, and at the timeout resets -- clearing what clearOnReset names through the app's clear callback and telling it to go home -- or only goes home, or nothing, as onIdle says; staff mode has no clock; a clear that fails leaves the kiosk failed. Hardware-key blocking is built on Linux: DVKiosk.enforce grabs every combo that leaves a kiosk through X11, riding the global-shortcut pump, filtered through the accessibility exemption so a kiosk blocks escape and never access, and reports what was held and what the server refused; verified under Xvfb with XTest, where Alt+Tab is swallowed and Tab is not. Fullscreen is asked of the GTK window when there is one. Declared policies parse with their refusals enforced -- a literal exit PIN, `auth` in a display-scope clearOnReset, an idle warning longer than the timeout. Exit attempts count to maxAttempts and lock out for lockoutFor, refusing even the right PIN while locked, and the lockout survives resume(). Enforcement resolves the specification's per-target strengths and reports DV-KIOSK-001, 002, 004 and 010; the runtime reports 003 and 005. The screen-side half is built: DVKioskHost turns any pointer or key into activity, shows the countdown while the runtime warns, sends the app home on a reset, and replaces the page with a diagnostics screen when the watchdog reports a restart loop -- which the Linux device binding does, counting startup arms and reporting the fourth in five minutes as DV-KIOSK-008 (restart-loop detection is therefore built); the watchdog itself restarts on a missed heartbeat and heartbeats systemd through sd_notify, which is what restart supervision under a systemd unit needs. Pointer confinement on Linux is built: DVKiosk.enforce holds the pointer inside the toplevel with a grab on the application's own X connection, verified under Xvfb with XTest warping the pointer outside and finding it inside. Notification suppression on Linux is built: the freedesktop notification the binding sends is held back while the kiosk holds, counted, and let through on release; the in-app inbox is not that binding and continues. System-gesture blocking is not applicable on an X11 desktop, which has no edge gestures to block. Kiosk windows in display scope are built under Multi-Window: DVWindowKind.kiosk, win.kiosk with state, enforcement, resetSession and exit, capability.displayKiosk. DV.Platform.display.kiosk is built: the generated runtime installs the declaration's device-scope policy at start, and the application observes the kiosk's state, reads what this platform honours, resets the session and leaves only through the declared exit method, the platform holding the policy on resume and letting go on exit. Native enforcement is built on the three desktops: Linux (XGrabKey, XGrabPointer, notification suppression), Windows (RegisterHotKey for the escape combos with the secure attention sequence and reserved keys reported unenforced, ClipCursor for the pointer, the window style for fullscreen; notifications never claimed) and macOS (NSApplication's presentation options, one fixed consistent set; a combo reported blocked only because the option covering it is in effect, Cmd+Q unenforced, pointer and notifications not claimed), each exercised on its own runner by the live suite; and on the web (Fullscreen, Keyboard Lock and Pointer Lock, each needing a user gesture and reported refused with the browser's reason when it is absent, a dedicated browser kiosk mode reported through the fullscreen display mode), exercised in Chrome by the browser suite. Android enforces natively now, and what stood in the way was a wrong conclusion rather than a wall: lock task mode belongs to an Activity, the application Context that package:jni hands back is not one, and that was recorded as the end of it. Application.registerActivityLifecycleCallbacks is the public route -- the callback is a Java interface, jnigen generates an implement for it, and the Activity in front of the person arrives in Dart with no platform channel. A declared device-scope kiosk also builds the launcher the specification names: the application becomes a HOME activity, or the home button leaves it, and it carries a device-admin receiver for dpm set-device-owner to point at, or lock task shows the "pin this screen?" dialog to somebody who is not standing there. Proved on the emulator that job has been booting all along: the kiosk is declared in that checkout, the build's own output is checked before the device sees it, the device is made the owner the way a kiosk is provisioned, an integration test asserts what the platform did, and dumpsys is read afterwards -- a Dart-side bool that lied would pass a test that only read it back. What is claimed is what lock task does: the home and recents buttons and the notification shade, wholesale, and no individual key combinations, so each declared combo is reported unenforced with that as the reason. This also found every Android binding dead in every real application -- the generated runtime's switch over the platform had no android case and its default reported success -- so clipboard, haptics and sharing were claimed and unreachable.  Native enforcement is built for eLinux now. There is no window manager there and no X11 -- the application draws on DRM and already owns the display -- so the enforcement is not about which application is on top, it is about the two ways somebody can get off it. A virtual terminal switch leaves the application running and puts a login prompt in front of it, on a unit in a lobby, and the application never finds out; the console underneath is still in text mode and paints kernel messages over the framebuffer while the application draws on it. Both are one ioctl each, both need CAP_SYS_TTY_CONFIG, which the generated systemd unit grants and a shell does not, and each is attempted even when the other fails since a device that allows one should hold the one it can. What was not held is named with the reason and carries DV-KIOSK-007, because a kiosk that could not hold and reports nothing reads exactly like one that did. Release gives back only what was taken, since an application that always releases on shutdown runs it on the path where the hold never happened. What CI can exercise is the refusal, which is the common path and the one that has to be right; the holding path needs a device with the capability. Absent: native enforcement on iPadOS, Tizen and webOS (DV-KIOSK-007 there). Built since: DVWindowKind.kiosk (display-scope kiosk windows, DV-WINDOW-010/011/012); deviceProfiles.<profile>.kiosk goes over the section in the generated DVKioskPolicies.device when dartvel build --device-profile selects that profile; dartvel inspect kiosk [--json] [--device-profile] prints the effective policy per target and per kiosk window with the source of each value (section, profile:<id>, policy:<name>, default). DVKioskPolicies.<name> is generated into the client's config from dartvel.kiosk.policies, each the section's settings with the named entry's over them; DV.lifecycle.kiosk is a read-only lifecycle signal the runtime drives and the kiosk host mirrors, so a reset shows as resetting -> active. DV-KIOSK-009 is built: dartvel doctor warns when onIdle: home has a model with a sensitive field in reach of an allowed route, naming both. kiosk.updates is built: apply reads immediate, maintenanceWindow or staffMode, window reads a span of the clock that may run past midnight, and the policy is in the path of every update: DV.Updates.check reads it -- with the staged rollout, the version lock and the skip -- and answers whether this device should apply this now, why not when not, and when it will be; DV.Updates.apply refuses what the check held back rather than quietly skipping it, and resets the session before a required update lands, which is what the specification says a forced update does outside the window. A maintenanceWindow policy with no window is a doctor problem rather than a kiosk that silently never updates. And dartvel build refuses to start when the declaration cannot be honoured, rather than leaving that to dartvel doctor: a pipeline that builds and does not run a doctor was shipping a literal exit PIN, green. Five containment keys the specification lists were read by nothing: routes.external, input.clipboard, input.textSelection, display.hideCursor and screenDim. The parser reads the routes, input and display maps and pulls three named children out of each, so those five were read straight past and dropped. Reporting them as problems by name was the first step -- an unrecognised enum value always produced one, an unrecognised key produced nothing, and that is the worse of the two, because somebody who writes input.clipboard: disabled into a kiosk has decided the clipboard is locked and silence reads as agreement. Four of the five are enforced now, and they are the four Dartvel can honour on its own in Dart with no platform binding. textSelection overrides what a page declares: the annotation is the page preference and the policy is the deployment decision, and a deployment that has locked selection has not left the question open to each page. clipboard refuses in both directions and before the platform binding rather than after -- blocking copy while allowing paste leaves a kiosk somebody can type into from whatever the last person left there, and asking the platform first would put the text on the clipboard and then report a failure. It refuses rather than doing nothing quietly, because a copy that reports success and copies nothing cannot be told from a broken clipboard. Neither is implied by kiosk mode: an order screen showing a reference number is more useful if the number can be copied, and the specification makes both explicit keys. What they deny follows the kiosk state rather than the process, so staff mode lifts it -- somebody with the exit method has been trusted with more than the person in the queue, and an engineer who cannot copy the error code off the screen reads it down a phone -- while a refused exit lifts nothing, or the way past a locked clipboard is to guess once. display.hideCursor is the third. A pointer nobody can move is what a touchscreen kiosk shows when the cursor is left on: it sits wherever the last mouse left it and reads as a frozen screen. auto is the default and means touch-only, which cannot be read off the build target -- a kiosk on a Linux box with a touchscreen is a desktop build, and a tablet in a keyboard case has a trackpad -- so it asks whether a pointing device is attached, and listens rather than reading once, because an engineer plugs a mouse into a kiosk to service it. always and never do not consult the hardware, since somebody who wrote always has a reason and a mouse plugged in for service should not undo it. The decision is a function in core of the mode and the hardware so the two halves cannot disagree, and the host applies it with a MouseRegion: the half Flutter owns, on every target that has a pointer at all, needing no binding that could be missing. display.screenDim is the fourth, and it is half of what the key asks for. A kiosk shows one attract screen for months and burn-in is what that does to a panel, so after the configured idle the surface is darkened and any touch or key brings it back; the backlight is not turned down, which needs a platform binding, and the field and the signal both say so rather than leaving a feature that looks like it saves power and does not. The dim is checked before the idle action and outside it, because tick returned early when onIdle was none and the one display that wants nothing but the dim would never have got it. The tap that wakes the screen is spent waking it: somebody touching a dark panel means come back rather than buy whatever is under a finger they cannot see. And a dim longer than the idle timeout is refused rather than accepted, because the reset returns the kiosk to its attract route and restarts the clock, so it never arrives -- ever, not merely usually. routes.external is the fifth and it is built now. What it needed was a meaning distinct from routes.allow, and the two keys ask opposite questions: allow picks which of this application's own pages the kiosk shows and defaults to all of them, while external decides whether an address that is not this application may be handed out at all and defaults to none. That default is the one that closes the escape hatch -- a footer link to the company website opened a browser on top of a lobby display, which hands the person an address bar and a machine. An entry on the allow list is an absolute URL: scheme, host and port match exactly, the path globs the way a route does, and a scheme with nothing after it -- tel: -- covers that scheme, which is how a kiosk gets a call-us button. Host matching is equality rather than a prefix, because example.com matched as a prefix also matches example.com.attacker.test. Enforced at the two points where a link actually leaves: DVLinkOpener, the funnel every DVNavLink.external goes through off the web, which returns without opening rather than throwing since a link the kiosk does not offer should do nothing when tapped and an exception out of a tap handler is a red screen nobody is standing there to clear; and on the web the interceptor, which prevents the anchor's default action before the browser follows it on the same click rather than deciding after the tab has opened. The refusal follows the kiosk state as the other containment keys do, so staff mode lifts it. Three declarations that cannot mean what they say are refused by the parser, which doctor and dartvel build already fail on: an allow list under external: block, where every address on it is refused while the list reads as agreement; allowlist with nothing on it, which is block under another name; and an entry YAML turned into something else, since externalAllow: [tel:] without quotes is a mapping and dropping it quietly leaves a list short by one. dartvel inspect kiosk prints every key the running kiosk acts on now rather than a subset chosen by hand -- clipboard, text selection, cursor, screen dim and the two external ones were enforced and invisible, so a kiosk that refused a link or a copy showed no line saying which declaration did it. DVKioskResetReason.startup and .staffExit are passed now, and neither was a label looking for an event. staffExit is the specification's own rule that resume() returns to kiosk and resets the session, which resume() did not do at all: staff mode is a state rather than an unlock, so coming back out of it is where the engineer's diagnostics page, their half-filled form and whatever they signed into stop being on the screen, and until now the next person in the queue inherited all of it. startup is the restart -- a kiosk is supervised on every target that can do it, so a crash mid-order brings the process back in seconds and the parts of a session that outlive a process come back with it. Which arrival it was comes from the state resume() is leaving, so no caller passes it and no caller can pass the wrong one; every other state returns to kiosk without a reset, because a second resume while somebody is part-way through an order must not wipe it, and a lockout still outlasts a resume. session.clearOnReset clears something now. The runtime always called a clear callback and neither production construction supplied one, so the default ran and the default's body is empty: the key parsed, doctor validated it, the reset fired with the right reason, and the set of things to clear reached a function that does nothing with it -- a customer signs in at a self-service screen, walks off, the kiosk times out, and the next person taps through into an account still signed in. Three of the five are the framework's own and are cleared: the client cache through the configured adapter, the auth session through signOut, and the shared store key by key with the reserved dv. and workspace. prefixes skipped, since those hold window layout rather than anybody's session. Scope decides how far the store clear reaches, which is the point of the specification's table: device scope owns the store, a display-scope kiosk owns only kiosk.<name>.*, so DVWindowKiosk carries the declared window's name -- the policy alone cannot say which prefix belongs to this window, and two customer displays running the same named policy own different keys. routes.allow blocks a route now rather than merely describing one. It parsed, doctor read it and scanned the pages behind it for sensitive fields, and DV-KIOSK-006 was registered for a route outside it being blocked -- and nothing blocked one, since allowsRoute had two callers and both were doctor. The gate is the router's global redirect, the one place that sees a deep link, an intent, an address bar and every in-app navigation alike, which is what the specification's rule about deep links not being an exit path requires. It is emitted for every project rather than only a kiosk one, because whether a kiosk is holding is a fact about the running process: a kiosk window carries its own policy and staff mode lifts the list while the same binary runs. The attract route is never redirected even when the list forgets it, because home refused and redirecting to home is a loop rather than a wrong page, on the one screen a kiosk always has to be able to show. Absent: the power half of screenDim, which is a backlight and needs a platform binding rather than a rule in Dart; a clipboard the operating system shares with another application on a desktop; the system cursor outside the application's own surface; and native enforcement on iPadOS, Tizen and webOS (DV-KIOSK-007 there), none of which can be built or verified without that hardware. Absent as well, and deliberately: clearing signals and forms. The reset's navigation home already destroys the page and everything context.signal hung off it, and what survives that is state a project kept elsewhere on purpose -- clearing DV.global would drop the API client registered at boot and stop the kiosk working ninety seconds in. So an application supplies its own clear callback for those, and doctor names them as a warning rather than a failure, because a kiosk whose session lives entirely in the page is correct as declared. Naming it beats a framework default that silently reaches neither.

A Dartvel application renders in a terminal, which it could not before: `flutter build bundle` reads the compiler configuration a project's build hooks need -- every Dartvel application has one, the Rust runtime -- and looks for it at build/flutter_assets/linux/x64/<mode>/CMakeCache.txt, which nothing writes. The desktop build writes one two directories away, so a terminal build runs that first and copies the cache across; it is a configuration step and nothing from it ships. Absent: the fork's own renderer -- the Kitty protocol with an ANSI fallback -- and a distributable runner. Both live in dartvel_cli_flt, a Rust custom-embedder project that no machine here has installed, so `dartvel build linux-cli` still stops at the toolchain check and says so rather than substituting a desktop build. Everything the Dart side owns is now wired end to end. Built: terminal size as a signal (DV.Platform.terminal.size, read from the attached terminal and again on SIGWINCH); DV.Platform.terminal.graphics, which is asked of the terminal rather than guessed from TERM -- Kitty's a=q query paired with a Device Attributes request so a terminal without graphics support answers no instead of timing out, with the reply reader treating a partial reply, an id that belongs to somebody else and an outright refusal as three different things; launch negotiation for a dual-mode build (arguments and display decide, the spec's wording asks when there is no display, a terminal outcome goes to the runner beside the GUI binary); a terminal-only build that generates a main for the binary it is actually producing -- `dartvel build <desktop>-cli` now carries its resolved backends to generation through --render, so the main declares the terminal alone, installs the surface at startup, and never goes looking for the -cli runner it already is; and DV.Window.open in a terminal, which navigates and reports DVWindowPresentation.page with DV-WINDOW-001 rather than asking an operating system for a window on a machine that has no display server

The performance contract is built: open() to ready (real and virtual), tear-out handover, shared-store write rate and coalescing ratio, store size and spill count, and restore-on-launch duration are measured; a call site that always degrades, a key written twice within a frame, a restore over the startup budget and owned windows outliving the frame budget on close are findings, one per subject; the running application publishes them beside its live window list and dartvel analyze performance aggregates degradations per call site, worst first. Built and tested: the generated runtime takes the single-instance lock at start, opens the arguments the process was launched with as external requests, hands a later launch's arguments to the first process and ends the later one (DVAppLaunch, wired through createDartvelRouter(arguments:) and the project template's main); window identity as canonical URL with idempotent open(), the window.open binding on Linux through dartvel_windowing (which is what flips capability.multiWindow), XRandR/Xinerama display enumeration behind window.displays, DVDisplayHint resolution that never falls back to another display, DV.Window.main with promotion, the exit policy (lastWindow/mainWindow/explicit, owned windows excluded), owned windows closing in reverse order with a closed owner refused rather than reparented, modality that degrades honestly where the OS cannot enforce it, the single-instance lock and external open requests draining into the running application, workspace restore dropping routes that no longer resolve, the reserved dv./workspace. shared-store namespaces, DV.Test.fakeWindowing, dartvel inspect windows, and the DV-WINDOW/DV-KIOSK registry behind dartvel explain, checked against this specification's own tables. Every code in the registry has an emitter: 001-013, with 006 the one error, raised when the claimed binding is missing or throws rather than filed under the OS declining (004). The live window list is built: the primary instance publishes what it has open beside its lock on every change, and `dartvel inspect windows` reads it while it is fresh and otherwise says the app is not running and when it was last seen. The Studio window inspector is built: a Windows tab in free Studio lists the window manager's windows live, each with a close. Kiosk windows are built: DVWindowKind.kiosk with a declared policy owns its display (another window asking for it is placed elsewhere, DV-WINDOW-011), is pinned (a close is refused, DV-WINDOW-012, until kiosk.exit satisfies the declared method), presents in place with its policy running when the display is gone or the host cannot pin (DV-WINDOW-010), and has a session of its own; capability.displayKiosk reports whether the host can pin. Still Designed: tear-out. Display enumeration is on all three desktops: XRandR or Xinerama on Linux, EnumDisplayMonitors with GetMonitorInfoW on Windows, CGGetActiveDisplayList on macOS, each through FFI and each decoded into the same spelling, so a panel name, a primary flag and a layout origin mean the same thing wherever they came from. Every one is exercised against the runner's own desktop session rather than asserted from a unit test: a display list that parses and describes no real screen is the failure worth catching, and only a machine with screens can catch it. Where there is no windowing layer at all the list falls back to PlatformDispatcher.displays, which reports no panel name, no primary flag and no layout origin. Device profile display names are carried into the generated client: dartvel build --device-profile becomes the DARTVEL_DEVICE_PROFILE define, DVDeviceProfiles carries every profile's display names, and the runtime installs the selected profile's before any window opens. dartvel.windowing.sharedState is read now, and was not: the specification documents four numbers under it and the build read none of them. Two are constructor parameters on the store already, with defaults equal to the documented values, so a project that set spillThresholdKb: 64 got 32 and one that set debounceMs: 200 got 50 -- accepted, built, and the number in the pubspec was decoration. Kilobytes there and bytes in the constructor, converted at the build, since passing the number through would spill at 64 bytes. Emitted only when a project tuned something, because the store is built lazily with its own defaults and replacing it with an identical one is a line that does what not writing it does; and a value that is not a number is dropped rather than emitted, since a typo in a pubspec should not fail a build with an error pointing at a generated file nobody wrote. A spilled object is deleted when the value that spilled it goes away, and nothing deleted them: removing a key cleared its pointer and left the object, and a value that shrank below the threshold was written inline over the pointer and left the object, so the bytes stayed on disk or in a bucket for the life of the installation with nothing referring to them. The object goes before the pointer, because a crash between the two leaves an object nothing points at -- which the next write of that key replaces -- while the other order leaves a pointer to an object that is gone, and a reader following it gets an error rather than a missing value. Absent: pollMs and sweepAfter. There is no separate-process polling backend, so pollMs has no parameter to reach. sweepAfter cannot be honoured for a sharper reason than having no sweep: DVFileStorageAdapter has list and delete and no notion of when an object was written, so "older than 24 hours" is not a question this interface can answer, and answering it would mean adding age to every adapter -- S3, R2, Azure, GCS, local and memory -- for one setting. windowing.web.inPageViews, windowing.web.openInNewWindow and windowing.android.freeform are read and honoured now, and were documented and read by nothing: the capability hard-coded what each platform can do, so a project that wrote openInNewWindow: false still reported multiWindow on web, still offered the control, and still opened a browser window when somebody pressed it. A declaration narrows what a target offers and never widens it -- a phone does not gain a second window by writing one down, because a capability that lied in that direction would be worse than one that ignored the setting: a caller would offer a control and the call behind it would degrade. Null is not declared, which is the platform's own answer rather than false, since defaulting to false would withdraw windowing from every application that never wrote the block; freeform: auto is the documented default and emits nothing for the same reason. Also absent: dartvel migrate-code, which ## Compatibility named as the way to rewrite the DV.Platform.Window sugar to the explicit form. There is no such command in dartvel_cli and no rewrite-rule list for one to run; the sugar is kept, so nothing needs rewriting, and the section now says so.

The entry here used to be a copy of Multi-Window's and described the wrong section. Built: the tab strip, reorder, tear-out gated on capability.tearOut with the gesture absent rather than broken where it is false, the empty-window rule, duplicate tabs with DVTab(route, duplicate: true), deduplication by route -- which was by object identity and only worked because const canonicalisation made two literal tabs the same object -- and persistence through persistWorkspace/restoreWorkspace with unresolvable routes dropped. Persistence is scoped: the stored layout is keyed by tenant and user as well as the workspace name, so one person's open tabs are not the next person's at the same desk nor the same person's in another tenant. The switcher is built: on a TV the strip is a row of tiles the D-pad moves between and select chooses, on a watch a stack to tap, and on both moving or closing a tab is an action on the tab's menu rather than a drag; the presentation follows the device and a page can name it. Re-dock is a handover rather than an adoption. Every window is a View in one ViewCollection under one build owner, so a tab carries a key of its own -- belonging to the tab, not to the workspace and not to the route, which is what keeps two deliberate tabs on one route from sharing a half-written form -- and moveTo takes it out here and hands it over there inside a single frame. The element is reparented rather than rebuilt, so the text someone was part way through typing, the place they had scrolled to, the controllers and the requests still in flight are the same objects on the other side. moveTo says which of DVWindowHandover.sameEngine and DVWindowHandover.shared actually happened, and a receiver that already had that route reports shared, because folding a tab into an existing one moves nothing. Absent, and not for want of trying: the drag itself cannot leave a window. A drag belongs to the window the pointer went down in -- the OS holds the pointer there until the button comes up, Flutter routes every move to that view, and the feedback under the cursor is clipped to it -- so at Flutter 3.44 no strip in another window ever sees the gesture, whatever the two windows share. Nor could Dartvel work out which window the cursor was over: it does not track where its windows sit on screen, deliberately, because on Wayland there is no window position to track. So a cross-window move is an action naming a destination from moveDestinations, on the tab menu a long press opens, and it is the arrival that is the real handover. Tear-out is still not one: the new window renders the route through the host route builder, so a torn-out tab is built from scratch and only the shared store crosses. The reparenting is covered by tests with two workspaces in one widget tree, which is the arrangement two same-engine windows are in; it has not yet been run against two real OS windows, which needs a desktop host with Flutter windowing enabled.

Nothing this section asks for is unbuilt; what is not free is Pro, in dartvel_studio_pro in the private enterprise repository, attached through DVStudioSection and the editor's hook and publisher seams so an open-source build has no tab that opens onto nothing. Free: five leaf node types (text, image, button, spacer, divider), the layout boxes, the inspector, undo and redo, publish and revert, code export. Approval before a page goes live is Pro: an editor's Publish submits, an approver's decision writes the page, both audited. Multi-user editing is Pro: the free controller publishes every mutation as a DVStudioEdit and applies one from elsewhere, and dartvel_studio_pro carries them between sessions over a transport with the page's presence channel, viewer/editor roles and an audit trail. Revision history beyond in-session undo is Pro the same way: dartvel_studio_pro keeps a numbered, timestamped, attributed copy of a page at every save and restores any of them from a History tab. Reusable components are Pro the same way: dartvel_studio_pro's Components tab saves any page node as a named template, places instances with fresh ids, and pushes a change to every instance across every stored page. Responsive breakpoints are built: a node carries mobile-first per-breakpoint overrides, the renderer resolves them against context.screen.breakpoint, and the export switches on the breakpoint rather than flattening to one width. The visual backend workflow builder is not absent but Pro: it moved to dartvel_studio_pro in the private enterprise repository and attaches through DVStudioSection, so an open-source build has no Workflows tab. A Figma import -- every top-level frame of a file becomes a DVPageDocument, editable in the builder and exportable as an ordinary @DVPage -- also lives in dartvel_studio_pro, attached the same way, with the frames' auto-layout, fills, text styles and image fills mapped onto the node properties the renderer already paints A box's layout is its direction and how its children sit in it: spacing, main-axis and cross-axis alignment are read from the document, rendered, exported into the generated source, and offered by the inspector. Before this every list and row came out with the framework's default gap packed to the start, whatever the document said, so a design could be described and not drawn. Borders and opacity are in the document's vocabulary, a border being one decision made of two values that apply and export together. And the export writes every style the renderer applies: it wrote two of the twelve, so a page with colours, sizes, corners and weights left the builder as an unstyled skeleton that compiled. The property table is now the single definition -- renderer, inspector and export all read it -- and a test hands the exported page to the analyzer, because text that looks right and will not build is found by the person who just pressed export. An image can be one the application holds rather than one it points at: DVImage.stored names a key in DV.FileStorage and the renderer reads the bytes through an ImageProvider, so the same key in a header and a footer is read once and two keys stay two images. A key with nothing behind it draws the placeholder rather than taking the page down, because a document outlives the storage it was written against. A page's image node says where its image comes from, which it could not: it described a URL and nothing else, so assets, files and stored bytes were unreachable from a page. It is read through DVImage's own reader, so a page node and a model field cannot come to disagree about what a source name means, and the export writes the constructor the page draws. A box says its padding on four sides, casts a shadow and scrolls its own axis. Each was a property the page could draw and the document had no name for: padding collapsed to one number, so a card padded 24 across and 32 down came out 32 all round; every card in every design has a shadow and none of them arrived, so imports came out flat; and almost every screen is taller than the device it runs on, so an imported design rendered the overflow stripe on the first screen. A shadow is one decision made of five values, the colour owning it the way a border's colour owns its width, and each padding edge applies the whole inset because a modifier replaces the padding it is given. The check that every layout property reaches the export asks whether the property changes the export rather than whether it adds an argument, since a flag can change which constructor is written. A text node says its typeface and its line height -- the import already wrote the family and nothing read it, so every imported screen came out in the default font, and paragraphs came out at the font's own leading. Line height is a multiple of the size, Flutter's own unit and the one that survives a change of size. A box can be painted with a gradient: two colours and a direction, the first colour owning the decision, which is what a hero band, a button and a card are painted with in every design system there is. The property table gained a text kind for a value that is neither a number nor a choice, and the check that every style reaches the export sets a property's companions alongside it, because some decisions cannot be stated by one property. A child of a stack says where it sits, an image says how it fills its box, and a box can round some corners and not others. Each was a design a page could draw and the document had no name for: a frame placed by coordinate came through as a heap in the top-left with the right sizes and the right colours, every image took the renderer's default so half of them were cropped or stretched, and a sheet rounded at the top came through as a floating rounded rectangle. Only the edges and corners that are named are written -- filling the others in with a zero would move a child pinned to one edge and square a corner the designer rounded -- and an unrecognised fit falls back to the default rather than refusing to render, because a document outlives the version that wrote it. An exported page imports the generated client from where the file actually sits: it climbed one level whatever the route was, so every nested page the builder exported reached lib/pages/dartvel_client and did not compile -- and the whole point of the export is that the result is ordinary code somebody can keep. Reading a document back from its own JSON is a copy now rather than a view over the same maps, which is what let an export rewrite the document the running application was still serving. A text node says how many lines it gets and what happens to the rest, which a design says per layer: a card title is one line with an ellipsis and a description is three, and a page that said neither pushed everything below a long title down the screen.

Nothing named. The dartvel inspect family is registered and runs against a real project: verified by running inspect, inspect routes, inspect models, inspect functions and inspect jobs on the site, not by reading the command table. The dashboard is one per application rather than one per target, and it is the backend's rather than the client's. Every generated page it carried -- studio, models, queues, cache, routes, outbox, policies, telemetry -- was a plain page in lib/pages with no guard, no policy and no role on any of them, compiled into every client the application ships. On web that is bundle weight, on mobile it is app size and review surface, and everywhere it is the admin inheriting the application's own guards, shell and theme, so a module declaring shell: override could change the chrome of the screen somebody administers from. One of those pages is the page builder, and the generated router prefers a stored Studio document over the compiled page by design, so an unguarded builder is a site anybody can rewrite. They declare a policy now and the guard behind it refuses when the application has configured nothing to answer with, which makes the default refusal rather than exposure. The backend mounts it at a path the project chooses, defaulting to a name that is a default and not a constant: a fixed admin path is most of why wp-admin is the most scanned URL on the internet, and a framework shipping one would have created that for every application built with it. A release build does not serve it unless the project asked, because an application deployed by somebody who never read this must not acquire an admin endpoint out of convenience, while development serves it with no configuration at all. A request that is refused because nobody signed in is answered exactly as a route that does not exist, down to the status number and the absence of any header naming it: an admin answering 401 where the rest of the site answers 404 tells a scanner that this host is a Dartvel application with a studio on it, and where, before anybody has typed a password. Everything under the mount is hidden with it rather than only the mount, since one asset answering gives it away for the sake of one file. A page claiming the mount is refused at build time with both the file and the setting named, because whichever registers second is unreachable and which one that is depends on generation order. The artifact exists now: dartvel build web-server writes the dashboard into the directory the server already read from, which no build step had ever created, so a project that turned the admin on used to get a 404 from a mount that was working correctly. It is a static page rather than a second Flutter application, because the backend serving it may be a container with no Flutter toolchain and no route to the internet; it loads nothing from another host for the same reason, since a dashboard that half-renders because a CDN is unreachable is worse than one that was never offered, and this is the page somebody opens when something is already wrong. Every reference in it is relative, so moving the mount to something private does not break it -- the setting that exists to protect the dashboard cannot be the setting that breaks it. What it shows is the project graph: the models, routes, backend functions and jobs the application declares, each with the file it was declared in. One dashboard for the whole application rather than one per build target, which is why it reads the graph, which has no target in it. Absent: the dashboard reads the graph the build captured rather than the running application, so queues, cache tags and the page builder are named in the specification and not in it yet. Also absent: the dashboard during dartvel dev. The dev server serves web/index.html straight from the project rather than a build output, so there is nothing at the mount until dartvel build web-server has written one; the way to see it today is that build followed by dartvel preview.

Absent: PDF export. Export.pdf, DVPdfOptions, the print stylesheet generated pages carry, backend rendering through the headless browser the web build already uses, and DV-EXPORT-001 to 003 are designed and unbuilt. What ships: Resumable imports chunk against a shared tested chunker that reads the header once, skips it as a row and attaches it to every chunk -- without which a worker handed chunk 2 of a CSV had no column order and resumable CSV import could not work at all. Scheduled reports parse their cron where the schedule is declared, so an unusable one fails there rather than silently never running

Still absent, and not buildable here. The Android Keystore row: there the key falls back to a file only the user can read, and DVAppKeyStores.describe says so rather than implying keyring protection; a hardware-backed key needs the Android SDK and a device or emulator. The Vault and KMS adapters the spec describes plugging in behind the same call: there is no resolver interface, so an external manager has to push values in through DVSecrets.configure rather than being asked for one, and writing the adapter against a real server needs that server and credentials for it. Redaction reaches logs and span attributes; the other surfaces in the sensitiveField exclusion set (analytics, AI context, public serialization, search) are not yet matched against resolved secret values. Built and exercised on their own runners: the Windows row -- the key sealed with DPAPI to this user on this machine, the sealed blob being what sits on disk -- and the macOS row, a generic-password item in the Keychain through the Security framework; and the Linux row -- the Secret Service through libsecret, keyring-backed, exercised in CI on a private session bus with an unlocked GNOME keyring rather than skipped -- the 0600 file store it falls back to, the chooser that picks on what answers, and dartvel key generate|rotate|status, which refuses to replace a key that exists, rotates deliberately recording both fingerprints, and never prints the key. Built on the web, in Chrome: a non-extractable WebCrypto key in IndexedDB seals the application key at rest, the sealed bytes being what IndexedDB holds. Also built: rotation hooks (DV.Secrets.onRotate fires when a resolver reports a new value, every hook runs even if one throws, the same value fires nothing) and DV.Test.withSecrets, which restores values and hooks after a test, on a throw too. Resolution now runs configured values, then the process environment, then .env, parsed by dvParseEnvContents in dartvel_core. Configured values lead so withSecrets is not defeated by whatever the developer has exported; the environment leads over .env so a file checked into a repository cannot shadow the machine actually running the process. The deploy gate had its own reader that did not know the export form and so failed deploys over secrets the runtime resolves; it now asks DVSecrets through dvResolveSecrets and drops the values again before returning. Secret values are struck out of logs and span attributes by matching the values DV.Secrets resolved, not by guessing at key names. That catches a credential inside a connection string under a key such as url, one quoted back by an upstream error, and one typed into a message by hand. PUBLIC_ values are left alone and values under eight characters are not matched, both documented on DVSecrets. The declaration manifest and the diagnostics are built. dartvel build parses dartvel.secrets before any generation, refuses a client-scoped secret without the PUBLIC_ prefix and, now, a backend-scoped secret spelled with it -- the generator decides by prefix alone, so that contradiction shipped the value while the pubspec promised it did not. DV-SECRETS-001 reports a backend-scoped secret reached from client code, DV-SECRETS-002 an undeclared name in client or backend code, and DV-SECRETS-003 a PUBLIC_ variable in an env file that no declaration justifies, which the prefix alone would have compiled into the bundle. One emitter writes env.g.dart for both the CLI and the build_runner builder, with tests: a backend value reaches neither the source nor the exported map, a public value round-trips, output is byte-identical for identical input, and a name that is not a Dart identifier is left out and reported rather than interpolated into the generated source. The web resolver returning nothing at all is pinned by tests that were checked by breaking it each of the ways that look like improvements.

Calling the clouds themselves, which needs credentials rather than code. dartvel deploy --functions writes a deployment artifact per backend function for lambda, cloud-run, container, edge, fly, railway and bare-metal, and refuses to ship an environment whose declared required secrets do not resolve

Nothing named. DV.$, dartvel sh and dartvel task all work, the last reading tasks from dartvel.tasks in pubspec.yaml -- verified by declaring one and running it, which is how the shell was found to be discarding the output of any command that exited quickly

Built: the half of a home widget that is Dart. @DVHomeWidget on any widget generates the page the specification describes -- a route at /widgets/<id> that centres the widget's content, which is what lets the widget launch the application at itself and a page navigate back to it -- and the application's list of them beside the router, for the packaging that puts them on a home screen. The annotation existed and nothing read it, so a developer could write it, build, run, and find no widget anywhere and no message saying why. The identifier is the class name in kebab case without the trailing Widget, one rule in one place, because a widget somebody has already put on their screen is found again by it and two spellings of the route is a tap that opens the not-found page; two widgets under one identifier are refused. dartvel build honours the specification's sentence about unsupported targets: excluded by default and said, with the names left out and the target that has nowhere to put them, or refused with DV-WIDGET-001 when dartvel.homeWidgets.onUnsupported is fail. A value that is neither is refused rather than read as one of them. Android is packaged now: a declared home widget becomes an AppWidgetProvider, the metadata a launcher reads before anybody places one, a layout, and a receiver in the manifest -- four things, none of which can be added at run time. It draws RemoteViews rather than the Flutter tree, and that is the platform rather than a shortcut: a home screen is composed in the launcher's process, which cannot host a Flutter engine, so a widget claiming to render Flutter would be claiming something Android does not offer. What the specification does ask -- that a home widget can launch and navigate to a page in the application -- is what the tap does: a deep link to the route Dartvel generated for it. That needed deepLinks.initial on Android, which needed the Activity, which is why it arrived with the kiosk work rather than before it; without it a widget's tap opened the application's home route, which is a shortcut and not a widget. WidgetKit is packaged now on iOS and macOS. A widget extension is a separate bundle, so the build writes one -- its Swift, its Info.plist and its entitlements -- and splices a target into the Xcode project that builds it, embeds it in the application, and is depended on by the application so Xcode waits for it rather than racing it. Only one way that goes wrong is loud: a project file Xcode cannot parse will not open. The rest are silent, and each is checked: a target that exists as an object and is not in the project's target list is never built and the app installs without it; an extension with no Copy Files phase into PlugIns is built into the products directory and never enters the bundle; without the target dependency Xcode may embed an extension that is not there yet, which fails on some machines and passes on others; and a second build that appended rather than replaced would leave Xcode two targets with one name. The Info.plist's NSExtensionPointIdentifier is the line with no symptom at all -- without it the target compiles, links, embeds and installs, and the widget never appears in the gallery, because the system never asks a bundle it does not recognise for anything. The App Group is claimed at both ends and derived from the application's own bundle id: the extension's entitlement lets it read the shared container, the application's lets it write there, and one without the other is a correctly signed widget reading an empty container and showing its placeholder forever. macOS signs Release with a second entitlements file, so both are written; and the application's own CODE_SIGN_ENTITLEMENTS is only set where it has none, since a macOS project is already pointed at DebugProfile.entitlements and overwriting that would take the sandbox off an application to add a widget to it. The URL shape was wrong as well. A class carrying the annotation is a home widget now. The generated list of widgets reaches something that reads it. home_widgets.g.dart has carried dartvelHomeWidgets since it was written and the barrel has always exported it, and nothing read it -- not the runtime, and not the build either, which walks the source files again for itself. What needed it is publish(), which takes a bare string: order_status instead of order-status writes under a key no widget asks for, answers true, and leaves somebody looking at a home screen that never changes. configureDartvelRuntime hands the list over now, beside the model, job and module registrations, and publish refuses an id that is not in it and names the ones that are. Thrown rather than answered false, because false is what a target with no home screen says and this is a typo that cannot work anywhere; and an application that declares nothing is left alone, since a test and an older generated client both have no list and refusing every publish there would break working code to catch a typo. The immediate refresh on Apple is built.
