Four of the six signals change; two did not until recently and one still does not. DV.lifecycle.kiosk is driven by the kiosk host and context.lifecycle.transaction by DV.transaction, both real. DV.lifecycle.app advances now -- booting when the generated runtime is configured and ready in the post-frame callback, because a router that is built is not a screen somebody can see, which is the same reason the startup profile measures the frame rather than the constructor. DV.lifecycle.build still has a setter called from nowhere but its own test. context.lifecycle.page has nothing that constructs a page context at all, so reading it throws. context.lifecycle.request now exists on a backend function that declares a DVContext parameter, and it changes -- received, executing, then preparingResponse or failed. It does not reach completed, because the response body may be a stream the handler no longer owns and reporting a request complete while it is still sending would be a state that lies rather than one that is missing. context.lifecycle.page reaches a signal that moves now. There was no lifecycle extension on BuildContext at all, so the line the specification writes did not compile in a page, and the getter threw for want of a signal nothing ever created: the enum, the signal type, the getter and its refusal message all existed and none of it was observable. Every generated page route now carries its own -- inside the route rather than around the router, because two pages are alive at once whenever one is leaving as the next enters. It moves through created, ready, active after the first frame, then disposing and disposed. DV.lifecycle.app reports the states the platform gives it now, and reported two of its ten: booting and ready, both set by the generated runtime while an application was starting, and nothing ever set another -- so an application observing it to save a draft on going into the background never saw backgrounded and one refreshing on the way back never saw the return, which reads as an application that is never backgrounded rather than a signal that does not say. Flutter reports it already and the mapping is where the judgement is. hidden is the background as much as paused, because Flutter sends it first everywhere and on desktop it is the whole of it: a covered or minimised window never reaches paused. inactive is not the background at all -- a notification banner, the app switcher, an incoming call, with the application on screen -- so it maps to nothing, since calling it backgrounded would flush an application state every time a message arrived. resumed is ready rather than resuming, being the settled state rather than the transition into it. Still produced by nothing and deliberately: resuming and suspended have no platform event that distinguishes them, iOS suspension not being reported to the process at all, and initializing, stopped and failed would need a distinction the runtime does not make. Absent: the states that belong to a data fetch and a route transition rather than to a widget -- resolving, loading, entering, leaving, inactive and failed are named here rather than emitted at moments that merely resemble them, since a page reporting loading when nothing is loading is worse than one that never says so. The build signal advances now, and did not: setBuild was called by nothing but its own test, so every observer saw idle for the whole of a build and could not tell one that was generating from one that had failed from one that never started. The reason was structural rather than an oversight. The registry was a static on DV in dartvel_flutter, the CLI depends on dartvel_core and deliberately not on Flutter, and the one signal whose subject is the build pipeline was therefore unreachable from the process that runs the build. It lives in core now and DV.lifecycle returns it, which is what the specification means by the CLI, Studio, the analyzer and external tools observing the same canonical state -- one object rather than two that agree by coincidence. dartvel build reports generating through it, completes on success, and fails on the paths that leave without an exception as well as the ones that throw, since a process that exits non-zero in silence leaves the signal on whatever stage it reached.

A backend function whose first parameter is a DVContext is now given one. It was not: DVContext appeared nowhere in the CLI, so the parameter was decoded from the request like any other argument -- the client supplied the context the specification says is injected, and the generated client asked for it. It is injected first and positionally now, excluded from the client signature, and carries a request lifecycle that changes. Absent: completed as a terminal state, for the reason given under Lifecycle Signals.

Built: the runtime registry -- DV.Modules with its ids, lookup that names the registered ones when an id is unknown, a read-only lifecycle signal per module, and paths resolved against the mount point -- and mounting at build time. The build reads dartvel.modules, finds each module's project, takes the module's own route base off and puts the mount point on (the standalone /products/:id is /store/products/:id mounted), and the parent's router serves the module's own generated page at that path; the routes are in the parent's route manifest tagged with the module they came from, which is what the sitemap, the route explorer and the web server's manifest read. A mounted module is generated before the parent, since the parent imports its generated client, and one mounted twice is generated once. modules.g.dart registers every mount and gives each a typed accessor, so DV.Modules.notes is the module the build mounted. A backend-only module contributes no pages; a bad mount or a missing source is a reported problem rather than a crash. The example application mounts a real module, so every runtime job compiles a mounted module's routes and registry. Built since: what a module compiled into the parent contributes is the parent's to run. Its backend functions are in the parent's router at the module's own paths -- which is what its generated client asks for, having been generated against its own project -- its cron functions are in the parent's schedule, its AI tools in the parent's tool table, and its models' tables are created by dartvel db migrate when its data mode is shared. Each file's import is measured from its own project, or a module's function would be imported from a package that does not contain it. A split-backend or federated module contributes none of it: those run in their own deployment, and a second copy built from the source beside the parent would answer with something nobody deployed and would run the night's work twice. Two functions claiming one method and path, or two models one table name, are refused rather than one of them silently losing. The export/inherit declarations are built: the module's own pubspec says what it exports and the parent's says what it hands down, both travel into the generated registration, and DV.Modules.<id>.global<T>() -- the view from outside the module -- reads an exported global out of the module's registry and an inherited one out of the application's, refusing anything else by naming the declaration that would allow it. Nothing read either declaration before, so a module that had written down exactly what it shares shared everything, and a field its author thought was private was already somebody's dependency. Default is empty in both directions, which is the specification's isolation; module code reading its own private globals asks its own registry directly. Built since: a module's assets are the paths that find them in the parent -- Flutter serves another package's files under packages/<name>/, so DV.Modules.<id>.asset() answers with the mounted path and a path the module never declared comes back as itself rather than as a guess -- and its pages are typed targets, named for the route inside the module rather than for the mount, so the same module mounted elsewhere keeps the names and moves the paths. The example application mounts a module with a real asset, and CI checks that the module's screen renders at its route in a browser and that its asset is in the bundle under its package path. The federated module manifest is built: a module publishes its identifier, version, routes, capabilities, assets, shell, auth, theme and data modes, public functions and signals, the parent version it needs and where it is served from, signed over a canonical form with ECDSA P-256, and the parent verifies it before mounting. The refusals are the point and each is tested: a manifest edited after signing, a valid signature by a key the parent does not trust, a document naming a trusted key it was not signed with, a genuinely signed module that is not the one being mounted, an older version replayed over one already accepted, routes that collide with the parent's own, a capability the target does not have, a parent too old for the module's constraint, and an empty key list, which refuses everything rather than waving it through. The manifest is generated from the module's own project by dartvel modules manifest, signed when a key is given, so it cannot go stale the first time a page is added -- and the routes in it are the module's own rather than any parent's mount, which is the mistake that reads as correct because it works in the application it was generated against. dartvel modules list prints what an application mounts. The federated deployment mode is built: the parent verifies the declared manifest against the keys it trusts before mounting anything, takes the routes, version, assets and location from the manifest rather than from the source beside it -- the deployed module is what answers, and building a second copy from source works until the versions differ -- and generates no import and no page for them, listing them in the route manifest with the location they answer from, for a route explorer and anything else enumerating what the application knows about. They are in the parent's route manifest and now in its sitemap and the web server's manifest too, which the specification asks for: a federated micro-site serves its own HTML and still appears in the parent's route index and sitemap. The parent has no page to render for those paths, so the manifest carries the address the module answers from and the server sends the reader there, substituting the matched parameters into the module's own route -- /store/products/7 arrives at the module as /products/7. The sitemap lists the path under the parent's own domain, because that is the address a reader was given. A location that is not an http address is not redirected to, signed manifest or not. An embedded module contributes none of this: it is compiled in, and sending readers elsewhere for a page this build contains would be a broken link with a 200. A federated module with no manifest, no trusted key, a manifest that is missing, signed by an untrusted key, for another module, or naming no location is refused with the reason and mounts nothing.  The four per-module modes are read and carried into the generated registry, so a module can ask what it was mounted as: shell inherit/extend/override/none, auth inherit/independent/federated/public, theme inherit/extend/override/isolated, data shared/schema-isolated/database-isolated/remote. A federated module's defaults are the ones its own deployment can honour rather than the parent's, and an explicit auth: inherit or data: shared on one is refused: there is no shared process to inherit a session from and no shared database, so the module would run with no session and read as a login bug. A backend-only module declaring a shell or theme is refused too, having no pages for either to apply to. The auth mode decides whether the parent's guard applies to the module's routes: inherit puts them behind the guard over the parent's pages, public leaves them open -- a documentation module mounted into an application everybody has to sign into is a documentation module nobody can read -- and independent and federated have their session elsewhere, so the parent's guard is not theirs to apply. This also found the guard over a whole application reaching nothing: `**/` requires at least one directory, so a _guard.dart directly in the pages directory was never matched by the router generator's own copy of the glob, which is authorisation that silently does nothing. The four per-module modes are applied at run time now, not merely known. Data decides what a module reads: DVModule.table resolves what a model actually queries and .database resolves where, so a schema-isolated module reads its own tables in the parent's database rather than the parent's -- which it did, silently, because both queried the same name. dartvel db migrate creates those tables under the same names, and a test asserts the migration and the run time agree on what a table is called, because they are in different packages and neither would notice the other changing. That claim was ahead of the code when it was written: the command executed nothing at all until the migration was made to run its statements, so what the test asserted was that two names matched, not that any table had been created. A module's generated models resolve through DVModuleData rather than a name written in at generation time, since the mode is the parent's decision and the model is generated before there is a parent; an unmounted module is its own application, which is what keeps dart test inside one working. The backend registers the modules it serves, which it did not: registration was in the client's bootstrap, so in the server process every module looked unmounted and its models resolved a table nothing had created -- and backend functions are where model queries actually run. Theme decides what a module's pages render in: a module declares its own through DV.Modules.<id>.useTheme, extend keeps the application's value wherever the module left the framework's default, and override and isolated are one branch because Theme replaces what descendants see either way. Shell decides what surrounds them: the page's own chrome, the module's around it, the module's instead of it, or none at all -- the module's own included, which is what a kiosk screen asks for. The router wraps a module's pages and nothing else, theme outside chrome so a module's header is painted in the module's colours. The split-backend mode is built: the parent declares where the module's functions answer, the generated registry carries it, and the module's own generated client asks the registry for its backend before falling back to the application it was compiled into -- so the same module standing alone calls its own API and mounted calls the service it was deployed to. A split-backend module with no address is refused, because its pages compile in exactly as an embedded module's do and the only symptom would be a 404 from an application that was built, deployed and looks right. dartvel doctor checks the modules a project declares, and a declaration the build cannot honour fails it rather than being carried on from: a module whose project is not at the path it names, or a federated one whose manifest is missing or will not verify, mounts nothing, and shipping an application without the section on a green build is how a rotated signing key goes unnoticed. A backend-only module has no pages by declaration and is not a failure, and a mode that fell back to its default is said rather than refused. The same check runs at the head of dartvel build, so a module that cannot be mounted stops the build rather than only the doctor. The example's module resolves and runs on its own, which the specification says a module is: it had no dependency overrides, so pub inside it failed on the framework's own hosted-versus-path constraints and the one module in the repository could be built only through its parent. dartvel modules manifest was run in it and signed: two routes, its asset under the package path, and the trust line the parent pastes. A module says what it needs -- dartvel.modules.<id>.requires for one built from source, the verified manifest's capabilities for a federated one -- and dartvel build --device-profile refuses when the profile does not provide it or a declared fallback, in the specification's own words. The decision was in the manifest verifier and no caller ever passed it a target, so an image built happily around a module that could not run on it and the first anyone knew was a device in a lobby with a dead section. A profile nobody declared is refused rather than assumed empty, which would refuse every module, or complete, which would defeat the check. The exports block is read and honoured now, and was read by nothing: a module that had written down exactly what it shares shared everything anyway, because a module compiled into a parent contributed its pages to the route index and its functions to the parent router whatever the block said, and an author who wrote pages: false was refused nothing and told nothing. pages and functions are honoured at the two places that consume them. The shared set is the plainly named one -- a mount's routes are what the parent takes and declaredRoutes is what the module has -- because the other way round is the design that produced this gap: a consumer that does not know the block exists then gets the right answer rather than the permissive one. A value that is neither true nor false is refused by name rather than falling back to the default, since pages: yes-please reading as true is how a module silently shares what that line was written to keep. Absent: what models: [Product] governs. What is read is dartvel.module.globals.export and dartvel.modules.<id>.globals.inherit -- globals, and only globals. The specification also writes a broader declaration on a module, exports with pages, functions and a list of models, and nothing reads any of it. That is the same failure the globals declaration had before it was built, one level up: a module that has written down exactly what it shares shares everything, because a module compiled into a parent contributes its pages to the route index, its functions to the parent router and its models to the parent migration whatever the block says. A module author who writes pages: false is refused nothing and told nothing. Named rather than half-built because two of the three meanings are not obvious -- whether models: [Product] governs which types the parent may name, which tables the migration creates, or both -- and guessing one would produce a declaration that appears to work and enforces something nobody chose. The per-module lifecycle signal moves now, and did not: it was created at discovered and moved by nothing, so an application waiting for a module to be usable waited forever and twelve states had one of them ever produced. What registering says depends on where the module runs, because calling every registered module active would be a claim the parent cannot make: a federated module is deployed elsewhere and whether it is up is not something this process knows. embedded and backendOnly are compiled into this artifact and running here, so active; splitBackend is active as well, its pages being compiled in with only its functions answering elsewhere; federated is mounted, the parent having it at a path and no way to see whether it is serving. A registration that declares no deployment stays discovered, since the registry has been handed something it cannot place. The build-time phases -- resolving, validating, loading, mounting -- are not emitted at run time, because the build did all of them long before the process started and a signal reporting resolving for something resolved at build time is theatre.

A generated page's favicon is now derived rather than linked as it was written: dartvel build web decodes the image the model or the project named, resizes it to 32, re-encodes it and names the file after a hash of its own bytes, so it can be served immutable and two models sharing a source share one file. A value the build cannot read off its own disk -- a CDN URL, an SVG, an ICO -- passes through untouched, because rewriting it to a name the build invented would point every page at a missing file. Three declarations reached one deployment each before this. @DVModel(favicon:) reached the web server's page resolver and nothing static, so a statically hosted site wore the shell icon on every product and article. dartvel.seo.favicon reached the server and no static page at all. @DVModel(schemaType:) was in the same state, so a static build labelled every product and job posting a plain WebPage, which is structured data that validates and says the wrong thing. All three now reach the written page: model first, then application, with the module level the specification names folded into the first because a module's models are generated from the module's own project. Absent, and named rather than half-built. First, the derivative of a row's featured image: that image is a URL the database supplied, so deriving one means fetching an arbitrary host during the build -- which makes the build depend on somebody else's uptime and on a CDN free to serve other bytes tomorrow -- or fetching it per request in the server, which adds a round trip to a page load in order to save one. Second, the on-demand derivative for web-server rendering: the favicon that path serves is still the raw declared value out of the generated spec. The build pieces are there, since a web-server build writes build/web and could derive into it, and what is missing is a way for the resolver to learn the derived name, because the spec values are compiled into generated Dart before any build output exists. Deriving the files without that would leave icons nothing points at, which is the same bug as a declaration nothing reads.

encrypted: true is honoured now. DVFieldCipher seals a field with AES-256-GCM under a keyring read from DARTVEL_FIELD_KEYS in the server process environment, the generator emits the seal at the bound parameter and the open in _fromRow, and a process with no keyring raises rather than writing plaintext. What that covers is the generated model's own read and write path, and nothing else does it. A value reaching the table another way is stored as it arrives -- a raw DV.Database.execute, a CSV import, a migration backfilling a column that already exists. A column written before the flag was added reads back as a decryption failure, since no dartvel db command rewrites one under a keyring. Rotation has the same hole from the other side: the ring keeps decrypting under a retired key, nothing re-seals the rows, so in practice the old key can never be dropped. Also absent: showInAdmin, which gates nothing. The generator justified that by saying there was no generated admin view yet, and that stopped being true: Model.Admin renders the same generated form, so a sensitive field is already excluded from the admin by the form that builds it and the flag has no separate set to gate. Meaning it would need a second set of controls, admin only, so a field could be visible to an operator and not in an application own form -- a real distinction nobody has asked for, and a flag that silently did what showInForms does would be worse than one that does nothing, because it would look like the narrower permission was being honoured. Last, found while wiring the encryption: the generated sync codec encodes with toJson, which keeps sensitive fields, so a model published across a DVModelSync transport carries them in the clear, including one the row itself holds encrypted. Encoding with toPublicJson is not the fix by itself, because the receiving side rebuilds the model through Parser.fromJson and a required sensitive field then arrives null and throws. Whether such a model should be refused by the transport or carried redacted with every sensitive field made nullable is a decision about the sync contract rather than about this flag, so it is named here instead of guessed.

nothing. `dartvel build web` writes a page per route, expands parameterised routes through the application's own resolvers, and gives each page its head tags, structured data and crawler-visible HTML. A model provider needs its data source reachable at build time, which is how static generation works everywhere; a provider that cannot resolve is named and skipped rather than ending the build

The pipeline the section describes is built, and it is one pipeline in dartvel_core that every server renders through: route resolved against the manifest's patterns with its parameters, page data resolved by the declared mode (awaited; cached for a ttl; served stale and refreshed behind the response; deferred to the client), visibility checked (hidden is 404, unauthorized 401, each the shell without the data), the head generated from the data (title, description, image made absolute against the site, canonical), structured data written as JSON-LD, the page's favicon selected, the crawler-visible text generated from the data, the Flutter bootstrap kept, and, with streaming on, the head sent as its own chunk. The resolver is generated: model_pages.g.dart, pure Dart beside the models, names where each public model page's rows are and which fields carry its title, content, image and published flag, and the generated backend builds the route's resolver from it over the application's database and starts its server with it -- so with spaRoot the built site's /users/ada is Ada's page when it is asked for, hidden when unpublished or absent. dartvel.web.server (pageDataMode, cacheTtlSeconds, streaming, cache) travels in the manifest. The kept pages can be shared: given any DVCacheAdapter -- Redis where the deployment has one -- they go there as JSON with when they were kept, so a second instance serves what the first resolved rather than resolving every page for itself, and the manifest's ttl is honoured (the backend's fallback built its cache before reading the manifest, so a declared five minutes lasted sixty seconds). A page is fresh for the ttl and servable stale for the stale window after it, both declarable; a lifetime of nothing is not written, which is what Redis says when it refuses an expire time of zero. Proven against a real Redis in CI: two connections, one cache, one resolve. Structured data is typed per model: @DVModel(schemaType: 'Product') travels into the generated page spec and becomes the page's JSON-LD @type, and a model that declares none is a Thing rather than a guess from the class's name. The declaration now reaches both servers rather than one: streaming split the page in preview and was buffered whole by the backend that ships, because the FFI layer gathers the body of anything not marked a stream; a federated module's location was written by the build and acted on by the backend while preview served the parent's own shell for the module's path; and dartvel.seo travels in the manifest as a site block, because rendering a route replaces the head block the build wrote into the shell, so every served page came back stripped of its description, its social image and its site name -- values the static target keeps. The site's values are a floor a page's own resolved data overrides, and a hidden or unauthorized page still gets neither. streaming: shell sends the shell's head -- every preload, the splash, a preload for each body script -- before the page data resolves, with the resolver started in the request's tenant zone at the same moment; the title and data-written head follow the data, then the body. The early part is what dvHeadParts leaves out of what data writes, and a test renders the same shell empty and full to prove that part is identical in both. The native test holds the data back until the early bytes have reached a socket through the Rust runtime. A guarded route, marked guarded in the manifest from the router's own list, is never sent early and keeps its status; a record found hidden or unauthorized after the flush is a noindex page with none of the data, and a resolver that throws gets the route's own page marked the same way. Each route's own deferred parts and first-frame images are named in the head a server sends: a web-server build writes dartvel_prefetch.json keyed by route pattern beside a shell it leaves alone, and both servers add the matched route's list to the part of the head that goes first -- the first write under shell, before the data. The preview server streams shell-first through the same core function as the deployed one, with the same guarded-route and noindex rules. Absent: rendering Flutter widgets to HTML, which the section does not ask for.

sections.section: Embedded, Television, and Extension Build Targets
sections.absent: tizen and vscode build but have never been run; fuchsia's engine does not build at 3.44.5; webOS and Sony eLinux ship a Dart below the 3.12 floor, so their embedders cannot resolve the example webOS, Sony eLinux and Fuchsia now skip rather than fail, each naming which wall it hit, so a target nobody can build stops reporting a failure about the wrong thing. Present: the two targets exist and are routed -- dartvel build sony-elinux-iso and -img resolve to the eLinux bundle build with a format, and the bundle itself is built and verified on a virtual device in CI. Absent: the image. Dartvel bundles no system-imaging toolchain, so after the bundle is built the packaging step reports DV-ELINUX-IMG and skips rather than writing something that is not a bootable image. That is the whole of it: a complete system image needs a root filesystem, a bootloader and a partition layout, none of which this repository has any of, and emitting a file with the right extension would be worse than the honest skip because it would look like the feature.

sections.section: App Store Publishing and Privacy Manifests
sections.absent: Built: dartvel publish takes a built application to Google Play, App Store Connect, TestFlight or Firebase App Distribution, declared under dartvel.publish in pubspec.yaml. Host support, then the tooling, then the work -- and here the work is an upload of a binary that took minutes to produce, so every refusal comes before it: a track nobody publishes to is refused rather than corrected to the nearest, because "staging" could mean internal or alpha and guessing puts a build in front of the wrong people; Play credentials that were never declared are refused rather than left to fastlane, which stops to ask and a pipeline has nobody to answer; App Store Connect is refused off macOS at the start rather than with "command not found" at the end of a long build. --dry-run prints the command instead of running it. The upload uploads and nothing else, because a publish that also promoted the build would be two things under one word. Designed, not built: privacy manifests and Play Data Safety generated from the model graph and the native binding manifest, with dartvel doctor reporting drift; store metadata and screenshots versioned in the repository, screenshots taken from declared goldens; credentials resolved by name through Secrets rather than held. Absent: the stores are driven through their own tools -- fastlane, xcrun altool, the firebase CLI -- rather than their APIs directly, so a machine without one is told to install it rather than having it fetched; no store has been published to from CI, which needs an account and a signing identity; and metadata, screenshots and staged rollouts are deliberately not touched.
